articles.title: How to self-host n8n
articles.author: ritoban@nutgraf.agency (Ritoban Mukherjee) , Ritoban Mukherjee
articles.content:
Frustrated by workflow limits and token-based billing on AI automation platforms? n8n is a “fair-code” automation platform that you can host on your own device or servers, free from the usage restrictions that plague cloud-based platforms.
We’ve covered n8n on TechRadar before, so head over to our first-time user guide and list of compatible hosting solutions if you’re looking for more information. For now, however, I’ll walk you through the exact step-by-step process of setting up a self-hosted n8n environment using Docker, Docker Compose, and a Linux-based virtual machine or server.
What you'll need for this setup
- A virtual machine, server, or NAS with at least 2 vCPUs and 4GB of RAM. Heavier workloads will benefit from more CPU cores and memory.
- A compatible version of Linux installed on your server or machine, such as Ubuntu, Debian, or Raspberry Pi OS. CentOS Stream, Fedora, and RHEL are also supported.
- Access to the Docker and Docker Compose repositories using your Linux distro’s package installer. All of this can be installed through the Linux terminal.
- A managed Kubernetes cluster if you intend to run production-grade workflows (optional).
Step-by-step installation guide for self-hosting n8n
1. Install Docker and Docker Compose
Power up your Linux terminal. Then update your Linux software catalog by running this command:
sudo apt-get update
This will update your software packages, install any necessary certificates, and prep the system for installing Docker. Once done, execute the next command to install Docker and Docker Compose, along with any dependencies your system needs:
sudo apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin docker-compose-plugin
You can manually confirm that your Docker engine is installed and running by executing this command:

docker --version 
docker compose version 
2. Write your Docker Compose file
Create a new directory for your n8n setup, then navigate into it:
mkdir n8n-compose cd n8n-compose
Now, you need to create a new .env file inside the new directory. It should look like this:
DOMAIN_NAME=example.com SUBDOMAIN=n8n GENERIC_TIMEZONE=Europe/London SSL_EMAIL=you@example.com
Make sure to replace these values with your domain name, time zone, and email address. If you’re running n8n locally on your device, you can simply remove the domain name, subdomain, and SSL email fields to leave only the GENERIC_TIMEZONE field in there.
Next up, we need to create a compose.yaml file in the same directory along with the .env file. It should read like this:
services:
n8n: 
image: docker.n8n.io/n8nio/n8n 
restart: always 
ports: 
- "127.0.0.1:5678:5678" 
environment: 
- N8N_HOST=${SUBDOMAIN}.${DOMAIN_NAME} 
- N8N_PORT=5678 
- N8N_PROTOCOL=https 
- NODE_ENV=production 
- WEBHOOK_URL=https://${SUBDOMAIN}.${DOMAIN_NAME}/ 
- GENERIC_TIMEZONE=${GENERIC_TIMEZONE} 
- TZ=${GENERIC_TIMEZONE} 
volumes: 
- n8n_data:/home/node/.n8n 
- ./local-files:/files 
volumes: 
n8n_data:
This maps n8n to port 5678 on your device and stores all your workflows, credentials, and encryption key in a Docker volume. Again, if you’re installing locally, you can simply remove the N8N_HOST, N8N_PROTOCOL, and WEBHOOK_URL lines.
In the same directory, create a local-files folder to store all your workflows:
mkdir local-files
3. Launch n8n
You can launch all your Docker Compose containers simultaneously using a single one-line command:
docker compose up -d
After about a minute or so, run this command to see if the containers are up and running:
docker compose logs -f n8n
You can now open the n8n editor at https://localhost:5678 on your local device using any web browser.
4. Create a n8n account
When you launch the n8n editor in your browser for the first time, it will ask you to create a new account. Enter your email, name, and a password with at least one capital letter and a number. Once you complete the form, you’ll become the instance owner, which is similar to a super-admin in n8n.
This will give your account full access to every workflow and credential, but you should still set up member-level accounts if you intend to have other people use your instance and want to track changes.
5. Build your first AI workflow
You’ll now be able to access n8n’s workflow editor. This is a node-based visual interface that looks a bit like a flowchart with the option to add triggers and actions to create complex automations. If you’ve used a tool like Zapier or Make before, it shouldn’t take you long to figure out the basics.
n8n lets you use the Execute step button to trigger different parts of a workflow during editing, which is useful in testing and troubleshooting. Once you’re confident that everything works, you can save the workflow and toggle it on so that it stays active.
FAQs
Is n8n open-source?
n8n isn’t open-source but free-to-use with certain limitations. It’s distributed under a fair-code license that lets you use the platform for personal or internal business workflows free of cost. If you wish to commercialize it as a consumer-facing product, however, you’ll need to pay for a commercial license.
Does it cost anything to self-host n8n?
There’s some cost involved in setting up a self-hosted n8n environment, but it’s much less compared to how much you’d pay with a cloud-based automation platform with a subscription. Your only expenses here are your hosting costs for the server you use, but even that can be removed if you have a powerful enough local rig that can run workflows on its own.
Does n8n come with its own database?
n8n comes pre-loaded with SQLite on with every installation, which is fine for internal use. If you want to run production workflows, however, I’d recommend switching to PostgreSQL, which can better support complex multi-user workflows.
How do I keep my n8n instance secure?
Make sure to run your n8n instance over an HTTPS connection instead of plain HTTP. If you’re using an external server or a local network that’s shared by other users, take extra care to keep your encryption keys secure and do not put them directly in your .env file. Depending on your server configuration, you can use a secret manager like Azure Key Vault or Google Cloud Secret Manager to avoid attackers from reading your API keys by scanning the source code in plain text.
Ritoban Mukherjee is a tech and innovations journalist from West Bengal, India. These days, most of his work revolves around B2B software, such as AI website builders, VoIP platforms, and CRMs, among other things. He has also been published on Tom's Guide, Creative Bloq, IT Pro, Gizmodo, Quartz, and Mental Floss.

articles.summary:
The fair-code automation platform n8n allows users to bypass cloud-based subscription limits by self-hosting their own workflow environments using Docker, Docker Compose, and Linux-based server infrastructure.

### Key Points
- Users require a server or virtual machine with at least 2 vCPUs and 4GB of RAM to run n8n effectively.
- The installation process utilizes Docker and Docker Compose to manage containers, volumes, and environment variables.
- n8n is distributed under a fair-code license, permitting free use for personal or internal business workflows.
- The platform includes a built-in SQLite database, though PostgreSQL is recommended for high-volume production environments.
- Security best practices include using HTTPS connections and managing encryption keys through dedicated secret managers rather than plain-text files.

### Why it Matters
Self-hosting n8n provides businesses and developers with a cost-effective alternative to subscription-based automation tools by eliminating token-based billing and usage restrictions. This approach grants users full control over their data and infrastructure, making it a scalable solution for complex, internal workflow automation.

articles.title: UK digital infrastructure investment hit £11.2bn in 2025
articles.author: Alina Maria Stan
articles.content:
Britain’s businesses put £11.2bn into digital infrastructure last year, roughly three times what the official measure had been reporting.
The jump in UK digital infrastructure investment did not come from a building spree.
Almost none of the difference is new money. The Office for National Statistics changed what counts on Monday.
What the ONS actually did
Its headline measure counts investment in telecommunications structures. On that basis, digital infrastructure investment in 2025 was £3.6bn.
The expanded measure adds data centre buildings, hardware, network software and radio spectrum permits. That produces £11.2bn.
The statisticians are blunt about what they have done. They are not identifying new investment outside existing capital formation data, they write. The expanded definition classifies a greater share of what was already there as infrastructure.
And it fell
Investment fell £0.5bn from 2024, a drop of 4.0%.
It still came third in a series running back to 1997. The direction last year, though, was down, as Tom Krazit noted for The Stack.
The longer trend runs the other way. By 2023 investment had climbed 51% above 2019 levels, while total UK business investment rose 19% across the same years.
Where the money sits
Two asset classes took 84.0% of it in 2025.
The larger is other buildings and structures, at £5.6bn, which is where data centre buildings and fibre and base stations land. That category has grown 83.8% since the start of the 2020 pandemic.
Software and databases took £3.8bn, up almost 95% since 2021, and now a third of the total.
The hardware line reversed
Hardware had been in long-term decline. In 2025 it rose 54.6%, an increase of £0.3bn, reaching £0.7bn.
That is its highest since 2006. The ONS attributes it to data centres expanding to support cloud computing and AI.
Why the old measure missed this
A data centre is not one asset. Its shell sits under buildings, its servers under hardware, its models under software and databases.
The old method looked at structures in the telecoms industry and found none of that. The new one extends beyond telecoms into data processing and hosting.
The ONS considered publishing and broadcasting, then left them out. They make content rather than the infrastructure that moves it.
The state has already reclassified them
The government designated data centres as Critical National Infrastructure in 2024, alongside energy and water supply.
Hyperscale facilities, built and run by global technology firms for their own use, accounted for around 63% of data centre development activity in 2025.
What is driving the demand
AI use among UK businesses with ten or more employees has gone from about 12% in late 2023 to 35% this year, on the ONS survey.
Around 69% of firms were already using cloud systems in 2023, which is what AI deployment runs on.
Oxford Economics found the number of UK data centres rose more than 400% between 2000 and 2024, Tom Rees reported for Bloomberg.
The pipeline is much larger
Barbour ABI counts 171 data centre construction projects that either started in the past year or are expected to start within five.
Industry figures citing that data expect UK data centre investment to reach £10bn a year by 2029. They put the current annual total at £1.75bn.
Public money is a small share, and rising fast
Government grants funded 5.7% of market sector digital infrastructure investment in 2024, worth £0.7bn. In 2023 the figure was £0.2bn.
That is the highest in the series. Across the whole period from 1995 to 2024, grants came to £3.7bn, against £0.5bn the government spent on communications assets it owns itself.
Most of the money is private. The market sector invested £11.6bn in 2024 and funded £11.0bn of that itself.
Telecoms operators account for a large slice. Ofcom put their fixed-network spending at £6.8bn in 2024, with 77% of it going into full fibre access.
The broadband programme slipped
Project Gigabit is a £5bn scheme, and £2bn of it went out between 2020 and 2025.
Nationwide gigabit coverage was meant to arrive in 2030. The 2025 spending review pushed it to 2032.
The constraint is power
AI may have to be rationed, Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey has warned. A shortage of energy capacity will limit how widely any sector can deploy it, he said, in comments Bloomberg reported.
Britain already has the evidence. An Essex data centre waited on a grid connection, and the water industry has warned about supply.
The same squeeze is pushing capital elsewhere. Southeast Asia is planning four times the data centre capacity it currently runs.
Britain keeps announcing anyway. London Tech Week brought a run of AI investment commitments in June.
What the ONS says about its own numbers
The release carries a warning most coverage has left out. The ONS writes that these are not official statistics, and that nobody should use them for policy or decision-making.
They are research into an alternative method, published as official statistics in development. The agency advises caution in using the data.
What it still cannot see
The measure excludes data itself, because no UK estimates exist yet, even though data is what data centres are for.
It does not count cooling systems, power distribution equipment or server racks either. The ONS says it will consider adding them.
There is also a classification hole. The statisticians file a property company that owns a data centre under real estate, so its spending never reaches these figures at all.
What comes next
The ONS plans to fold the expanded definition into its main infrastructure publication, once the OECD reaches an international consensus on measuring these assets.
It is also building an AI account to track AI-related investment across the economy. Britain has meanwhile been funding sovereign AI through the private market.
Until the definition settles, the size of the buildout depends on which measure anyone quotes.

articles.summary:
The Office for National Statistics has updated its methodology to report £11.2 billion in UK digital infrastructure investment, reflecting a broader classification of data centers and hardware.

### Key Points
- The revised ONS measure includes data center buildings, network software, and radio spectrum, significantly increasing the reported investment total from the previous £3.6 billion figure.
- Despite the expanded definition, actual digital infrastructure investment fell by 4.0% in 2025, a decrease of £0.5 billion compared to the previous year.
- Data centers and software now dominate the sector, accounting for 84% of total investment as businesses scale cloud and AI capabilities.
- Government grants for digital infrastructure reached £0.7 billion in 2024, marking the highest level of public funding recorded in the series since 1995.
- The UK government designated data centers as Critical National Infrastructure in 2024, with 171 construction projects currently in the development pipeline.
- Energy capacity constraints and grid connection delays remain significant barriers to further infrastructure expansion, potentially limiting widespread AI deployment.

### Why it Matters
This reclassification highlights the growing economic importance of data centers and AI-ready infrastructure within the UK's national accounts. However, the ONS warns that these figures are currently experimental and should not yet be used to guide formal policy or major investment decisions.

articles.title: China's biggest apps are inviting the West closer into its insular internet economy
articles.author: Aditi Bharade
articles.content:
For decades, China's internet economy has been a gated-off party. Now, some of its biggest companies are cracking the door open to outsiders.
While China has long since invited foreign businesses to set up shop within its borders, its internet has been closed off. Dominated by a handful of local players — such as Tencent's messaging app WeChat, ByteDance's TikTok-equivalent Douyin, the X-like Weibo, and the lifestyle content app Xiaohongshu — the country's internet has been difficult for non-Chinese users to access.
Many of these platforms have historically been Mandarin-first and presented registration, verification, and other hurdles for foreign users. Because China's digital payment ecosystem is integrated into these social media apps, payment in the country is a challenge for foreigners, too.
But recent developments have pointed to a trend of China finally opening its doors and letting foreigners take small steps into its internet economy.
Paying as a tourist in China is becoming a lot easier
China has for years been largely cash-free in its major cities, and is known for its seamless payment ecosystem, which includes major players like Alipay and Weixin Pay.
Now, one big player is helping tourists make payments more easily while traveling in the country.
On August 11, PayPal announced that US PayPal users can use the service to make in-store QR payments at Weixin Pay merchants across China, without needing to download additional apps or set up a Chinese bank account.
Weixin, also known as WeChat, is owned by the Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent. Tencent's cross-border payment platform, TenPay, provides the underlying payment services used by Weixin Pay.
"Through our collaboration, international visitors will be able to use their home wallets to make QR code payments at tens of millions of Weixin Pay merchants in the Chinese mainland, offering them a familiar and convenient way to pay," TenPay CEO Wenhui Yang said in the PayPal press release.
Jeffrey Towson, the founder of US- and China-based retail consultancy TechMoat Consulting, told Business Insider that it was "almost impossible to be a tourist in China" without WeChat Pay or Alipay, and PayPal and WeChat Pay's integration largely solves that problem.
Allison Malmsten, a public research director at Daxue Consulting, a China-focused strategy consultancy, said that for decades, China had developed its own banking system and firewall, which made it seem like "China's digital universe existed separately from the rest of the world's digital universe."
She told Business Insider that the integration of PayPal into WeChat, among other examples, shows that China is playing a bigger role globally.
Opening up its famously closed-off internet
China's social media is inviting foreigners in, too.
The latest example is Bilibili, China's youth-focused content platform known for its popularity among anime, comics, and gaming enthusiasts, which has just begun its international expansion.
Bilibili started an X account this month. It announced in a Wednesday X post that it had just launched its international app, with access for "more countries" coming soon.
Semafor reported on Thursday, citing new job listings and marketing materials distributed to creators, that Bilibili is courting non-Chinese creators and recruiting staff in Japan, the US, and Europe.
Bilibili is the latest Chinese video-sharing platform to court non-Chinese users, following TikTok's overseas launch in 2017 and RedNote — known in China as Xiaohongshu — gaining a large international audience in 2025.
RedNote became popular last year, during a period when TikTok's future in the US was uncertain, as the app faced a "divest-or-ban" mandate. Many Americans flocked to RedNote instead, some calling themselves "TikTok refugees."
Towson said that TikTok proved that Chinese mobile apps could succeed outside the country, and now, every Chinese company he talks to has an international plan. This is partly because domestic consumption is stagnating and, in some sectors, slowing, prompting companies to seek new growth across borders.
"Every company I know is talking about international. Bilibili, I was not talking about this seven years ago. So, that's definitely a big trend," Towson said.
Racing to the global stage with its tech offerings
PayPal and Bilibili's developments come amid the backdrop of Chinese tech companies, in fields like AI, robotics, and electric vehicles, competing with the US for global domination.
Chinese startup Moonshot AI made waves in the global tech sphere with its latest Kimi K3 open-weight AI model, which promises "frontier intelligence" for tasks such as coding, knowledge work, and reasoning at a lower cost. As AI costs become a major concern for businesses, capable open-weight models like Kimi K3 are becoming highly sought after.
Jacob Cooke, the CEO of Beijing-based e-commerce consulting firm WPIC Marketing + Technologies, said he sees a trend of Chinese tech and internet companies having globally competitive offerings, "whether it's Kimi K3's frontier AI or Bilibili's unique content ecosystem."
"In Kimi K3 case, you have frontier AI available via open weights to build customized applications, and it's a fraction of the cost of Western models. That's a very attractive offering for Western enterprises," Cooke said.
"These firms are making aggressive, intentional forays into foreign markets to tap into foreign demand," he added.
articles.summary:
Major Chinese technology companies are increasingly opening their digital ecosystems to international users through new payment integrations and global platform expansions to drive growth beyond domestic markets.

### Key Points
- PayPal announced on August 11 that U.S. users can now make QR code payments at millions of Weixin Pay merchants across China.
- The youth-focused video platform Bilibili has launched an international app and is actively recruiting creators in the U.S., Japan, and Europe.
- Chinese tech firms are seeking international expansion as domestic consumption stagnates and competition for global market share intensifies.
- The lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, known internationally as RedNote, has gained significant traction among foreign users seeking alternatives to other social media platforms.
- Moonshot AI recently released its Kimi K3 open-weight model, offering Western enterprises a lower-cost alternative for advanced AI tasks like coding and reasoning.

### Why it Matters
These developments signal a strategic shift as Chinese tech giants move to integrate their services into the global digital economy to offset slowing growth at home. By lowering barriers for international tourists and courting foreign creators, these companies are positioning themselves as competitive, globally accessible alternatives to Western platforms.

articles.title: CNET Finds 75% of US Adults Couldn’t Care Less About a Foldable iPhone
articles.author: Dashia Milden
articles.content:
Apple could release its first foldable iPhone in a few weeks at the company’s annual September event (which could be Sept. 9). The late summer showcase is usually Apple’s big reveal for new hardware. The center of attention could be the rumored iPhone Ultra, Apple’s first foldable.
Analysts say the phone could be dubbed the iPhone Ultra (previously nicknamed the iPhone Fold and iPhone Flip). It’s expected to be a tiny iPad that folds in half, into a regular-size iPhone when closed. Rumors suggest Apple’s folding phone will feature a wide book-style fold, similar to the original Google Pixel Fold and the recently released Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8, which has a folding display with the same aspect ratio as an iPad.
The iPhone Ultra could also have two rear-facing and a single front-facing camera that works whether it’s folded or not, and come with Apple’s usual features and services. Analysts expect the phone to cost between $2,000 and $2,500, which is on par with, if not a little higher than, rival folding phones from Motorola, Google and Samsung.
However, most US adults say they aren’t interested in buying a new foldable phone.
A CNET survey that polled 2,605 US adults found that 75% aren’t interested in buying a foldable Apple device. Even if they bought one, they wouldn’t shell out thousands of dollars for it.
Key takeaways
- Three out of four US adults (75%) are indifferent about buying a foldable Apple device, such as the rumored Apple iPhone Ultra.
- US adults would spend an average of $781 on an Apple foldable device, which is a stark contrast to what analysts say the phone could cost (and $48 less than the base model iPhone 17).
- The RAM shortage is affecting nearly half (41%) of US adults’ plans to upgrade their phones. Some are holding onto their current devices longer than originally planned.
Most US adults don’t want a foldable iPhone
CNET found that most US adults, regardless of age, aren’t interested in a foldable iPhone. Older generations (Boomers and Gen X) express the least interest — 83% and 77%, respectively. Younger generations aren’t that excited either, with nearly 70% of Gen Z and millennials (69% and 68%, respectively) not interested in a foldable iPhone. And those who are excited about one aren’t willing to break the bank for it.
Patrick Holland, CNET’s director of content, finds it surprising that only 75% weren’t interested in a foldable iPhone. “Foldable phones are niche products, and it’s impressive that 25% might be interested in an Apple folding phone,” said Holland. “That would be a killer product debut if Apple could get that many people to buy one.”
The same thing can be said for the iPhone Mini and Plus models for those who want a smaller or larger screen, but still want an iPhone. Or the E series, which is a budget-friendly model starting at $600 before discounts.
Holland pointed out that the foldable iPhone isn’t meant to replace the baseline model; it’s about expanding the line and offering phone models at an even bigger price range. Apple could have an iPhone model at ever $100 increase between $600 and $2,000.
US adults will spend an average of $781 on a new foldable iPhone
On average, US adults are willing to spend $781 on a new foldable iPhone. That’s less than what most iPhones cost now. For context, the base model of the iPhone 17 starts at $799 (with a $30 carrier discount).
Gen Z is willing to spend the most on a foldable iPhone — an average of $919 — whereas other generations would spend less. Millennials would spend an average of $859, Gen X would spend $690, and Boomers even less — $572.
“The fact that people want an average price that’s nearly $50 below the baseline iPhone 17 shows where we’re at financially right now,” said Holland. “A foldable iPhone is going to be expensive to make, and its retail price will likely reflect that.”
But foldable phones haven’t always been this expensive. Holland points out that the price of foldable phones has dropped for years, as with the Motorola Razr line. The first model cost $1,400, but last year you could buy a new one for half that price before discounts. Now those prices have started to rise again (because of the RAM shortage), and the rumored $2,000 price for the iPhone Ultra is proof of that. It’s a few hundred dollars more than foldable phones cost just a couple of years ago, Holland said.
The RAM shortage is affecting iPhone upgrade plans
The evolution of AI and data centers has led to a memory chip shortage — also known as the RAM shortage or RAMageddon. Personal devices, like phones and laptops, need those chips for data storage. However, the shortage has led tech companies to raise prices on their devices.
Apple raised prices on many of its devices in June for this very reason. The RAM shortage and price increases are making 41% US adults rethink their plans to upgrade to a new iPhone — regardless of whether it’s a foldable or another model.
“The very companies investing in AI and building data centers to support new features and tools on phones are the ones passing the higher cost of RAM and chips on to consumers,” said Holland. “There’s a corporate Gift of the Magi happening, and it’s us who are footing the bill while companies rake in record-breaking profits.”
Many contemplating an upgrade are weighing other options due to price increases. Some are considering older or less expensive options (5%) and switching to another brand (4%), while others are considering refurbished or used models (4%) to save money on the upgrade. Others (9%) will only upgrade if a trade-in or a mobile carrier promotion covers the price, which usually comes in the form of account credits or a multiyear commitment to stay with that carrier.
The bigger story is that most US adults aren’t eager to upgrade due to the RAM shortage and device price hikes. Ten percent are planning to delay their upgrade and keep their phone longer, while 9% are holding onto their phone longer than originally planned.
Twenty-two percent of US adults don’t plan to upgrade anytime soon, regardless of Apple’s new devices or the impact of the RAM shortage. By generation, 19% of Gen X and 27% of Boomers don’t have plans to upgrade anytime soon, while 16% of millennials and 21% of Gen Zers share the same sentiment. Here’s a breakdown.
If you have an old phone and the battery is the only issue, replace it instead of getting a new phone, Holland said. “You’ll add another two to three years of life onto your phone and avoid paying hundreds of dollars more for an upgrade or multiyear commitment to a carrier.”
If you’re still thinking of upgrading your phone, Holland said the best deals on phones are typically found when a new model launches or during holiday sales. And even though trading in your old phone is a good way to save money, check with third-party reseller sites, too.
“You might be able to get more money for your old phone than from the carrier or phone-maker is offering,” said Holland. “Used and refurbished phones are definitely worth buying, as are models from a year or two ago, and often discounted by hundreds.”
Lastly, be skeptical about that “free” $1,000-plus phone a carrier is willing to give you. These deals often come with multiyear commitments and are shown as account credit rather than cash. If you switch to a new mobile carrier before the phone is paid off, you’ll have to pay the difference.
Methodology
All figures, unless otherwise stated, are from YouGov Plc. The total sample size was 2,605 adults. Fieldwork was undertaken between Aug. 13 and 17, 2026. The survey was carried out online. The figures have been weighted and are representative of all US adults (aged 18 and older).
articles.summary:
Apple may unveil its first foldable smartphone, the iPhone Ultra, at its September event, though consumer interest remains low due to high projected costs and current market trends.

### Key Points
- The rumored iPhone Ultra is expected to feature a book-style folding design similar to the Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Google Pixel Fold.
- Analysts estimate the device will retail between $2,000 and $2,500, significantly higher than the average consumer's preferred price point of $781.
- A CNET survey of 2,605 US adults found that 75% of respondents have no interest in purchasing a foldable Apple device.
- A global RAM shortage is driving up hardware costs, causing 41% of US adults to reconsider or delay their planned smartphone upgrades.

### Why it Matters
The potential launch of a high-priced foldable iPhone highlights a growing disconnect between Apple’s premium hardware strategy and the financial constraints of the average consumer. As memory chip shortages drive up device prices, many users are opting to retain older phones longer, signaling a challenging environment for luxury tech adoption.

articles.title: The 4 Best Car Phone Mounts I’ve Tried (2026): Belkin, Andery, Andobil
articles.author: Matthew Korfhage
articles.content:
A car phone mount is no longer an option—it's a necessity. Nearly every US state restricts cell phone use while driving (we see you, Montana!), and most require full hands-free operation. The best car phone mounts offer an easy view of your phone's screen without blocking your view of the road, hold your phone securely, and keep vibration to a minimum.
I've spent weeks and hundreds of miles testing car phone holders for iPhones and Android alike, on busy freeways and on potholed city roads. What I found is that the best car phone mounts aren't necessarily expensive or name brands: They're just smartly designed.
The best car phone mount for an iPhone is almost always a secure MagSafe mount. The one I keep in my car when I'm not testing other mounts is a sturdy, compact Andery suction mount ($36) that holds preternaturally fast to both my phone and dash but can also be mounted to a window. My favorite mechanical car phone holder for Android phones is a sturdy, versatile, ball-joint mount from Andobil ($30) that affixes tightly to a car's dash, windshield, or air vents.
Here are the best car phone mounts for each car and phone type. See also WIRED's guides to the Best USB Car Chargers, Best Portable Jump Starters, Best iPhone Cases and Accessories, Best MagSafe Accessories, and Best Wireless Phone Chargers.
Best Car Phone Mount for iPhones and Qi2 Phones
The world is full of bulky phone mounts that block your view of the road, inflexible phone mounts that only allow for horizontal or vertical mounting, weak suction cups, and kinda mid MagSafe attachments. And then there's this innovatively designed, wonderfully compact dash and window mount from Andery.
On flat surfaces, the nano-gel suction cup holds fast like Hodor at the door. The 22-magnet MagSafe ring allows airflow to avoid overheating, but it also holds stronger than most comparable Qi2 magnets. And unlike bulky plastic mounts, the Andery's aluminum-arm, stainless steel ring keeps a low profile and interferes minimally with one's line of sight. In fact, when affixed to my dash, this device doesn't block my view of the road at all. The ring rotates 360 degrees. The two-joint arm can either fold tightly to the mount or extend outward. No other mount I've tested combines all of these virtues.
But note you'll need a relatively flat surface to get a good bond with the suction cup. I've also seen some reports that the suction cup can lose adhesion over time if repeatedly re-mounted (and it's cussedly difficult to remove in the first place, though it leaves no residue when you do). Non-Qi2-compatible Android phones will need a MagSafe case to be compatible with this car phone holder. But if your phone has a magnet or a magnetic case, this is the simplest and most effective car phone mount I know, and it performs leagues better than other similarly designed car mounts like this one from Acer.
Note also that Andery offers a Qi2-compatible phone charger version at the expense of airflow. I haven't tested this variant yet.
Best Universal Car Phone Mount
Mechanical mounts like this one from Andobil—with holders that can be slid in sideways to securely grip the phone—are flexible for a broad range of phones and don't require MagSafe technology. But they're also mostly bulky, making them a less preferred option as a windshield or dashboard mount because this will block your field of vision.
Among all similar devices I've tested, this one from newer Chinese company Andobil is the most compact I've tested when not in use, while still offering a lot of flexibility. The nanogel suction cup on its dash mount is one of the most stable I've tested (almost aggressively stuck on, to be honest). And the extendable arm, while plastic, feels less cheap and breakable than other models. The kit also comes with an air vent mount, whose three-point design makes it among the most stable vent mounts I've tested and allows you to maneuver the phone so it does not block the vent.
This mechanical car phone holder is hard to call aesthetic. It's essentially a pad with a gripper on the side. But the grips extend to accommodate even larger phones and are able to keep the phone in place even during vigorous shaking. (If you're wondering whether I place phones in these phone mounts, and then come at them like they're a shake weight? I do.) The release button's a little awkwardly placed, and Andobil's marketing about “military standards” is a little silly on a low-cost device made with thermoplastics. But after I watched other suction cups wilt in summer heat, this Andobil's still going strong.
★ A Great, Low-Cost Air Vent Mount: If you're mounting only to your air vent, the Vanva air vent phone mount ($13) is among the cheapest mounts of any kind that I've tested, while ranking among the most secure mechanical mounts. (Actually, I like the mechanical phone holder a bit better than Andobil's.) The lockable clamp affixes easily and securely to most vertical or horizontal-slatted vents—and unlike hook-based vent mounts, it's easy to install and remove. The multi-joint ball arm can be maneuvered so you don't lose airflow from the vent, and the adjustable grips that lock in your phone can be released with a simple button press. This Vanva is a relatively flimsy plastic device, so I don't rule out that it might break someday. But its inexpensive replacement cost makes this an acceptable risk.
Best Car Phone Mount With Charger
Look, I'll be honest: I have mixed feelings about chargers on car phone mounts. The mount will have to be plugged into a car charger anyway—and at that point, I might as well just plug in the phone directly, which will usually lead to faster charging.
But convenience is in the eye of the beholder, and many people prefer to just leave the car mount plugged permanently into a car charger so they never have to worry about their phone draining while navigating on a mapping app. For y'all, here's the car mount from ESR, which offers decently fast 15-watt charging and a cooling fan to mitigate phone overheating.
The suction was effective when attached to both my window and dash, and the device is compact enough to not much hinder my field of view. Charging speed is merely moderate, enough to charge an older iPhone in a couple of hours. ESR also offers a faster-charging Qi2.2 device for twice the money, though I have not tested it.
★ A Good, Stylish Vent Charging Mount: Most vent chargers plant themselves directly into the airflow of your vent. But not all of them do. WIRED editor Julian Chokkattu recommends the Peak Design Car Vent Mount ($100). The mount stays secure on the vent, but an arm allows the charger a little distance from the vent. It's also a little bit stylish, a rarity for vent mounts. If you're using a Pixel or Samsung phone, we also like Peak Design's MagSafe phone cases.
Best Minimalist Car Phone Mount
Most people don't overwhelmingly want their car vent mount to be a defining feature in their car's interior. This Belkin takes this notion to the extreme. This silver and black air vent mount is minimalist, svelte, and—dare I say—almost classy. It grips phones surprisingly securely for a phone mount without feet to support the phone's bottom, according to WIRED reviewer Simon Hill, and you can rotate easily from portrait to landscape. There's also a handy rubber clip to hold charging cables in place. Just note that this will not be the best option for larger or heavier phones.
★ For larger phones: The Kenu Airframe Pro ($30) has a similar design but is built to accommodate thicker cases and larger phones, noted WIRED tester Simon Hill. The ball-and-socket joint allows 360-degree rotation and also lets you angle your phone for better viewing. It's a bit less sleek, however.
How I Test and Select Car Phone Mounts
Car phone mounts are and are not a sensitive technology. Bulky mounts can block your field of view while driving. And it's a genuine safety hazard if your car mount, or your phone, falls on the floor while you're driving down the freeway.
Every phone mount I and other WIRED testers recommend has been road-tested against this possibility, driven for hours on the road, and on long road trips, over sometimes bumpy roads. Often, I kept as many as eight devices at a time glued to my dash, windshield, and vents so that my car looked like a dollar-store communications center. For the most recent round of testing, this included multiple days of relatively humid, 90-degree Fahrenheit heat.
I pulled suction cups off of dashboards and windshields, over and over, to see if suction cups wore out the first time you had to move a device—or if the cups left residue on the windshield. I tested using multiple models of iPhone, a long folding Motorola Razr, and a large-model Nokia, onto each mount to see how it held up—with or without bulky cases.
I clamped each phone in and out repeatedly, to see how easy it is to remove a phone from the mount. I also turned each mount upside down and shook vigorously to see how violent I had to be to shake the phone loose from its mooring.
Where chargers were involved, I tested the charging capacity with ammeters and phone apps, as well as simply by marking how long it took to charge my phone compared to other chargers. I also tested the MagSafe charging speed vs. the speed if I'd just plugged the phone directly into my preferred USB car charger. (The USB always wins, for multiple reasons.)
For the most recent round of testing, I tested a dozen phone mounts during a sticky summer, selecting both best-selling and best-recommended mounts from both well-known brands and a new breed of hyper-specialized brands like Andobil and Andery that have made their name only on car phone mounts. My colleague Simon Hill likewise tested a dozen mounts in a previous round of testing.
Can Android Phones Use MagSafe and Qi2-Compatible Mounts?
MagSafe is a great technology for the more than half of cell phone owners in the US who use Apple products. The best phone mounts, with the fewest compromises, are pretty much all magnetic mounts.
But alas, most makers of Android phones have been more resistant to adding magnetic mounting capability. The Google Pixel 10 is an exception and offers built-in magnets and native Qi2-compatible charging support. Other phone makers, like Samsung, offer MagSafe-compatible cases for newer models like the Galaxy S26 series.
Some makers of MagSafe mounts offer little stick-on devices meant to affix to your non-magnetic phone. Don't bother with these; they don't work that well and don't stay affixed for long. If you'd like the convenience of a magnetic mount, you're going to have to get a MagSafe-compatible case for your phone. And for this, I refer you to WIRED's guide to the Best MagSafe Accessories.
Honorable Mentions
Belkin 15W MagSafe Mount for $80: This Belkin MagSafe charger and vent mount is an older device we've recommended previously as a top pick—with a secure magnet pad that offers 15-watt Qi2 charging. The mount positions itself in the air vent and blocks airflow a bit, but on summer days with the air-conditioner running, this positioning can help cool your phone while it charges. It's also a little bit sleek but also a bit on the spendy side for what it offers.
Andobil MagSafe Air Vent Mount for $37: This vent-mounted MagSafe device looks like a charger but isn't. The mount's broad, flat surface does stabilize the phone a bit. But in trade, it blocks airflow both to the phone and from the air vent. For these reasons, it's not really my favorite design. But the magnet is strong enough to hold the phone in place, and the vent mount is also stable.
iOttie iTap 3 Air Vent Holder for $16: This compact vent mount from iOttie is low-cost, and the MagSafe mount is strong enough. I can hold this thing upside down and shake it without dislodging my phone. But there's very little range of motion, and the phone can only be mounted where it'll block airflow from the vent. I also tend not to favor mounting mechanisms that use hooks, because it can make the mounts more difficult to remove when needed—though for unusual air vent geometries, the hook might be the only style of vent mount that works.
iOttie One Touch Dash and Windshield Mount for $28: This dash and windshield mount from iOttie was a favorite of WIRED tester Simon Hill when he tested it two years ago. But there's been a design update and some reports of durability issues, so until we test the newest model, I'm leaving this in the honorable mentions.
Vanmass Car Phone Holder for $40: Similar to the Andobil I recommend as a top pick, this Vanmass is a ball-socket mount with options for air vent or dashboard/windshield mounting. But it's a bit bulkier than the Andobil, and the air vent mount is a hook-based mount—which I tend to find more difficult to remove. The suction cup on the dash/windshield mount is ridiculously strong and is unllikely to dislodge even on hot days—and didn't leave residue when I removed it. But while Vanmass advertises “military-grade” tech, whatever this means for a phone mount, the plastic felt a bit flimsy, especially on a vacuum locking mechanism for the suction cup.
Bokilino Car Cup Mount for $16: This is a different sort of phone mount than most I tested: It affixes to a standard cup holder and holds up your phone like a liberty torch from atop a bendable gooseneck stem. This is all well and good when you're driving solo, notes WIRED reviewer Kat Merck, but during longer trips with family, it takes up a much-needed cup holder, and the stem can get in the way. In most cars, you'll have to look a bit too far away from the road to see the screen.
Not Recommended
Acer Gadget Car Phone Mount for $28: This little car mount from Acer mirrored the design of my top-pick Andery but fell far short on performance. The suction cup pretty much walked off the job after I removed and replaced it once, the magnet isn't as strong, and the mounting arm is shorter and doesn't rotate. There's no particular reason to buy it in a world where the Andery exists.
iOttie iTap 3 Dash and Windshield Mount for $25: MagSafe car phone mounts from iOttie have one chief merit: The magnet is strong and secure, unlikely to dislodge on even the bumpiest roads. But alas, the same cannot be said for the suction cup on this bulky dash and windshield mount, which gave up the ghost on a hot day.
Scosche Magic Mount for $13: This is maybe the most compact, low-cost MagSafe device I tested. Its S-branded design is both unobtrusive and winningly inscrutable: It looks like a talisman Jor-El might have brought back from Krypton. It's also the one with the weakest magnet. My iPhone lurched off at minor provocations.
iOttie Wireless 2 Qi Charging Phone Mount for $50: Don't mistake “Wireless 2 Qi Charger” for a Qi2 charger. A couple of years back, this MagSafe charging mount was a top pick for WIRED, but the charging is now a bit sluggish by modern standards.
articles.summary:
Selecting the right car phone mount is essential for safe, hands-free navigation, with top-performing models like the Andery MagSafe mount and Andobil mechanical holder offering superior stability and design.

### Key Points
- The Andery dash and window mount ($36) is the top choice for iPhones, featuring a strong nano-gel suction cup and a low-profile aluminum arm.
- For Android users, the Andobil ball-joint mount ($30) provides a versatile, secure grip for various phone sizes on dashboards, windshields, or air vents.
- The Vanva air vent mount ($13) is a highly recommended, budget-friendly option that uses a secure, lockable clamp rather than fragile hooks.
- ESR offers a charging car mount ($15W) for users prioritizing battery life, though direct cable charging remains faster and more efficient.
- Minimalist options like the Belkin air vent mount provide a sleek aesthetic, while the Kenu Airframe Pro ($30) accommodates larger devices.

### Why it Matters
Using a reliable, well-positioned phone mount is critical for complying with hands-free driving laws and maintaining a clear line of sight on the road. Investing in a high-quality, stable mount prevents the safety hazards associated with devices falling or obstructing the driver's view during transit.

articles.title: One year with the Google Pixel 10 Pro Fold: Sometimes it's good to be boring
articles.author: harish.jonnalagadda@futurenet.com (Harish Jonnalagadda) , Harish Jonnalagadda
articles.content:
It took me a while to like the Pixel 10 Pro Fold; I didn't like that Google basically retained the same feature-set as the Pixel 9 Pro Fold and just added a bigger battery and IP68 ingress protection. At 258g, the Pixel 10 Pro Fold is one of the heaviest foldables — only my Huawei Mate XT is heavier, and that's basically a tablet that folds down to a phone.
The heft notwithstanding, the Pixel 10 Pro Fold has other issues: the cameras are underwhelming compared to the Vivo X Fold 5 and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra, battery life is average, and cellular connectivity isn't quite as stable as I'd like. But having used the foldable on and off for the better part of a year now, I will say that it is much better to use than its specs would suggest, and the software continues to be among the best around.
Software matters
Google's software is why I used the Pixel 10 Pro Fold instead of other foldables. I like the bright colors and customizability that's available in Material You, and Google does a great job with the interface in general, delivering a clean UI without any clutter. And with the 10 Pro Fold, Google optimized the software a little better, and there's better fluidity than in previous generations, which makes a noticeable difference when navigating the interface.
Magic Cue is one of my favorite additions, and I like that it pulls up any contextual detail without me having to dig for it. Whether that's sharing waybill details when calling DHL about recent deliveries or surfacing reservation details, it is genuinely useful. Google does a good job bringing most Gemini features to other phones, but there are a few exclusive to Pixels, like Magic Cue.
The software has gotten better with Android 17, and Bubbles multitasking is easily my favorite feature. It's annoying that it won't be coming to other phones, but the floating windows mode makes it easy to maximize the real estate of the 8-inch inner panel, and I use it constantly. Other foldables do a great job with multitasking in general — ColorOS' Open Canvas is the gold standard — and while Google should have stolen the feature, it's good to see some progress in this area.
Shining bright
I also like the size of the cover screen; the 6.4-inch panel is slightly wider than its predecessor, and it's the ideal size. While Google had its share of screen-related issues in the past, I didn't see any problems with the outer or inner panels in the year I used the Pixel 10 Pro Fold. Both panels are among the brightest in the category, and they have good color vibrancy.
After a year of unfolds, the crease hasn't deformed, and the hinge articulation is just as smooth as the day I set up the device. A lot of that has to do with IP68 dust and water resistance. While I didn't submerge the foldable in water, dust ingress is a constant problem on these devices, and thankfully, I didn't have to worry about that in the slightest.
Get the latest news from Android Central, your trusted companion in the world of Android
Not quite point-and-click
With plenty of tuning updates over the course of the year, the cameras on the Pixel 10 Pro Fold still don't pass muster. It has been a regular source of frustration with the foldable, and in a year where other brands made huge strides in this area — the X Fold 5 and Find N6 have outstanding cameras — the 10 Pro Fold is distinctly second-best.
I carry two phones, and for most of the last 12 months, the secondary phone was the iPhone 17 Pro, so I had an alternative whenever I needed to take photos. That doesn't make it any less annoying that a $1,799 foldable can't take reliable photos or videos.
Rounding out
The 10 Pro Fold is heavy enough as it is, so I didn't bother with a case. The foldable took its share of tumbles, but it is unscathed. There are some scratches that have accumulated over the course of the year, but on the whole, the Gorilla Glass Victus 2 protection did its job. If anything, I don't put a case on any phone that has Victus 2, and it's proven to be reliable — at least in the way I use my devices.
While I didn't think much of the design, the rounded corners definitely make a difference. They make holding the 10 Pro Fold a little easier, and there's enough thickness at the sides to open the inner screen. This is an issue on the Galaxy Z Fold 7 and the Z Fold 8 Ultra, and not just because they're thinner — the X Fold 5 and Find N6 are just as easy to unlock as the 10 Pro Fold. I'm chalking it up to the way Samsung designs its foldables.
I'll admit that the Pixel 10 Pro Fold doesn't have the best internals. It's continually annoying that Google prioritizes other areas like the TPU instead of CPU and GPU performance, and this means the Tensor G5 isn't suited for playing demanding games.
That said, it held up a lot better than I imagined. While I test visually-intensive games as part of a review, I don't play high-end games on my phone all that much, and the ones I actually play the most — Balatro, Ball x Pit, and CloverPit — run without any issues. There is some overheating with gaming sessions lasting over an hour, but that's the case with every foldable, and not unique to the Pixel 10 Pro Fold.
Another bugbear is connectivity. The Exynos modem that Google went with isn't as good at maintaining a signal, so I frequently saw cellular connectivity issues while at home.
The single biggest annoyance with the Pixel 10 Pro Fold proved to be the cameras. Other than that, the foldable was better than I imagined. Thankfully, I didn't run into many software bugs; outside of Magic Cue getting disabled by an update, I didn't notice any problems. I know that's an outlier considering the thousands of messages on Google's troubleshooting pages, but it hasn't been much of an issue in my usage.
While I enjoyed using the Pixel 10 Pro Fold, I wouldn't necessarily recommend the foldable. There isn't a single feature that truly stands out, and while that's not a bad thing, it doesn't make for an exciting phone.
Look, I generally prefer Google's software and don't mind some of the annoyances that come along the way, but it may not be what you're looking for in a device that costs over $1,700 — particularly when there are better all-round choices available.
If you're a Pixel fan and are considering a foldable, I'd suggest getting the 11 Pro Fold; I'm switching to it now, and it addresses a lot of the 10 Pro Fold's issues around imaging. And if you don't have a brand allegiance and just want to try out a book-style foldable, the Moto Razr Fold continues to be fabulous.
Harish Jonnalagadda is Android Central's Senior Editor overseeing mobile coverage. In his current role, he leads the site's coverage of Chinese phone brands, networking products, and AV gear. He has been testing phones for over a decade, and has extensive experience in mobile hardware and the global semiconductor industry. Contact him on Twitter at @chunkynerd.

articles.title: 24 npm Packages Abuse unpkg Mirrors to Host Fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA Pages
articles.author: info@thehackernews.com (The Hacker News)
articles.content:
Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new campaign that uses a cluster of 24 npm packages as free phishing infrastructure for redirecting to ClickFix-style fake CAPTCHA pages.
"While the malware is simply a single HTML page inside the npm package, and while downloading it wouldn't do harm, the threat actor’s use of npm isn't to infect developers who install it, but to use the registry and its mirrors as a safe, validated storage for the malware," OX Security researchers Moshe Siman Tov Bustan and Vitalii Chepurko said.
The list of npm packages, some of which are still available for download, is below -
- bgzxcuite2
- prezdentkxheiw
- egair0810
- mnteckets
- airdzticket
- egypt0811
- passport811
- vxhjkseuiaqkb
- ndmushdkeqe
- ndmxchdjxn2
- ndmfguyhoxc3
- mjsdqwocvn
- m2fcsfyjkuxb
- m3fdfocdoewn
- @worrisome/reutil
- testdgdbcsd
- tesgfvbncsdbcv
- mndsxcusiwlk1
- mn2adskhweox
- mn3sadkoiewu
- mn4xcouzvhus
- mbxcnsuwgs1
- skxcmwuncbg2
- mobiwaefhxc3
The campaign specifically targets mirrors like unpkg. Once mirrored on these services, the HTML file (e.g., "unpkg[.]com/ndmxchdjxn2@1.0.0/index.html") becomes a live, fully-rendered fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA page that's hosted on a trusted domain but redirects to attacker-controlled phishing infrastructure that could enable ClickFix attacks or credential harvesting.
As a result, anyone who opens a link that's hosted on the npm mirror will be tricked into carrying out unintended actions that can lead to the deployment of malware. This involves displaying a fake Cloudflare verification page, which then sends the target to an external website controlled by the attacker.
The HTML page embeds the logic to serve the bogus CAPTCHA verification prompt, as well as JavaScript necessary to send a request to a remote server. Initial iterations of the malware were found to send the request to a typosquat domain that impersonates the Microsoft login page ("login[.]microsofte[.]live").
But after the domain was added to Google Chrome's Safe Browsing blocklist, the threat actor behind the campaign is said to have responded by switching to KeyVal ("api.keyval[.]org"), a free, public key-value store that allows developers to set a key-value pair or retrieve a value given a key using a REST API.
In doing so, it turns the legitimate service into a dead drop resolver (DDR) and uses it to extract and decode the URL to which the victim is redirected to.
"Currently the remote logic transfers the user to the legitimate ChatGPT website, but it could be weaponized to deliver ClickFix or any other phishing domains when configured to by the attacker," the researchers said.
This is not the first time this approach has been abused by bad actors. In October 2025, Socket detailed a set of 175 npm packages that used unpkg.com's content delivery network (CDN) to host redirect scripts that routed victims to credential harvesting pages as part of a campaign codenamed Beamglea.
"Threat actors keep finding and using new and novel techniques not just to deliver malware, but to use legitimate infrastructure to store their payloads and data," OX Security said.
"When we think of malware as families of code that steal data directly from the machine they are running on, we can miss other ideas such as infrastructure abuse, using npm and its mirrors as free storage, and persistence – since npm packages can live forever in mirrors even after they are removed from the official stores."
articles.summary:
Cybersecurity researchers have identified a campaign using 24 malicious npm packages to host fake Cloudflare CAPTCHA pages on trusted CDN mirrors for credential harvesting and phishing attacks.

### Key Points
- Researchers at OX Security discovered 24 npm packages serving as free, validated storage for phishing infrastructure.
- Attackers leverage npm mirrors like unpkg to host HTML files that display deceptive CAPTCHA prompts to users.
- The campaign uses the legitimate service KeyVal as a dead drop resolver to dynamically update and hide malicious redirect URLs.
- Initial iterations of the attack targeted a typosquat domain impersonating Microsoft before shifting to public key-value storage APIs.
- These packages remain accessible on mirrors even after removal from the official npm registry, providing persistent hosting for attackers.

### Why it Matters
This campaign highlights a growing trend of threat actors abusing legitimate software supply chain infrastructure to bypass security filters and host malicious content. By turning trusted services into storage for phishing payloads, attackers can effectively evade detection and maintain long-term persistence for their operations.

articles.title: OpenAI's Sam Altman just admitted he was "wrong" about AI — laments that he made the tech seem "scary"
articles.author: jez@windowscentral.com (Jez Corden) , Jez Corden
articles.content:
The big AI era isn't going as some might've hoped.
OpenAI and other big companies are losing billions chasing artificial intelligence technology, and it's only clever accounting and circular investments keeping the entire industry afloat. OpenAI specifically is in hot water, with spending commitments through to 2030 coming scarily close to $1 trillion dollars, and is operating purely on the basis of handouts from the likes of SoftBank, NVIDIA, Oracle, and Microsoft. OpenAI is looking to spend $50 billion in compute alone in 2026 on roughly $25~ billion in revenue, revenue which is also made up at least in part with IOUs.

Despite the scary numbers, OpenAI is trucking along on faith and fumes alone, as companies' belief in the tech keeps the firm alive, for now.
Yet, even Sam Altman is having doubts about the impact of large language models. In a new podcast, Altman lamented "economic inertia" for the lack of adoption, and also called out the AI industry for making the tech seem "scary."
"A lot of the people building AI have been off saying there's a 25% chance we're going to destroy the world ..."
Altman effectively blamed those pesky humans for not adopting ChatGPT and other AI products, lamenting that "people keep using their tools in the same way" they had previously been using them.
"I thought when we got to [ChatGPT]-4, which was back in 2023, I thought very quickly after that there'd be much more disruption, with the software business up for grabs right away. I was wrong about a few things, one of them, in terms of the speed ... the economy just has so much inertia. People keep doing the same things they're doing, they keep buying from the same company, they keep wanting to use their tools in the same way ..."
Altman implied that the "slow" pace of change would make the "transition" to AI "smoother." Elsewhere in the podcast, Sam Altman remarked that AI leaders had "not done a very good job" explaining AI tech, referring to the broad backlash to the technology.
"I also think a lot of the people building AI have been off saying there's a 25% chance we're going to destroy the world ... and yeah, we're going to race ahead and do it because otherwise those bad guys will do it first. Or it's like, 'man, this thing is going to be really terrible, and 50% of the jobs are going to go away in the next year, and we hope you are all okay,' but it seems really scary.
We have not, as a field, done a very good job of explaining to people what the benefits are and how the downsides can be mitigated. We certainly have not done a good job ... even if people have had answers like, 'well, there's going to be universal basic income, or work will be optional', or whatever. There's been very little discussion from people about how and why it's important that people have more power and freedom in the world, not less."
My take: Altman just doesn't get it
I think the key issue with this AI tech is that most people just don't find it very useful. I work in an industry that, at least on paper, should benefit from some kind of automagical writing tool. The problem is that it loses so much nuance and accuracy that, even if I wanted to use it for work, I literally can't.
I think a lot of these very technical, mathematically-inclined dudebros pushing this format have little knowledge or understanding about how and where this technology should be applied. Spotify, YouTube, Instagram, gaming platforms, and other services are actively trying to filter out AI content, as it is repeatedly proven to decrease engagement — users actively hate it. Companies that are using tokens to try to boost productivity are finding that they're actually just boosting costs, and that they're simply finding a new bottleneck in the finite amount of addressable customers.
LLMs undoubtedly have uses, but when 90% of the compute is being spent on utterly unproductive use cases, the economics simply seem primed to implode. If you're spending tokens for the sake of spending tokens, and it doesn't lead to any discernible increase in sales — what is the point? You could use AI to make hundreds of slop video games, but people already have more than enough to play built by an ironically more affordable human workforce.
RELATED: Ed Zitron talks to us about Microsoft, OpenAI, and the future
In the future, I think we'll find AI probably ends up as a tool of governments in things like law enforcement and medical fields. Specific industries will benefit from tools that can parse and summarize large, complex data sets, albeit with the unfortunate knowledge of LLMs' penchant for hallucinations and outright lies. Just yesterday I asked Copilot to find some links to some old Windows Central articles I did. It just straight up lied and gave me some completely made-up links instead. Extrapolate these simple mistakes to medical fields or military applications, where lives are literally at stake ... is it worth the risk?
Perhaps the issue is that AI's inaccuracy renders it only viable in low-stakes businesses ... and those low-stakes businesses simply won't see a real return over doing things the "old way," which Altman describes as economic "inertia."
Perhaps it's not inertia. Perhaps the AI business model is just not the disruptor it was cracked up to be.

If companies cannot prove that these tools provide tangible value beyond experimental use cases, the industry may struggle to justify its massive capital expenditures.

articles.title: Bitcoin Crosses $80,000 For The First Time Since May Amid Crypto Bounce Back
articles.author:
Siladitya Ray, Forbes Staff, 
 Siladitya Ray, Forbes Staff
 https://www.forbes.com/sites/siladityaray/
articles.content:
Topline
The price of bitcoin rose past $80,000 late on Monday, leading a continued rise in the price of major cryptocurrencies that began last week amid interest in the so-called “debasement trade” after the Treasury intervention in the bond market.
Key Facts
The price of bitcoin—the world’s most valuable cryptocurrency by market cap—rose to $80,453 early on Tuesday, up more than 25% in the past week.
This is the first time since mid-May that bitcoin has crossed $80,000—but it is still well below the all-time peak of $126,000 reached last year.
Ether, the second-most valuable cryptocurrency by market cap, rose to $2,503 early Tuesday, up more than 30% from the previous week.
The crypto rally helped boost other major tokens, with Solana’s SOL, Binance’s BNB, XRP and the memecoin DOGE rising 32%, 18.7%, 51.7% and 31.8%, respectively in the past seven days.
What Do We Know About The Debasement Trade?
Last week, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced he would double the Treasury’s buyback of long-dated bonds in a bid to curb rising yields. The move came after the 30-year Treasury yield rose to its highest level since 2007—amid concerns about the war in Iran and the U.S. national debt hitting $40 billion. The move prompted a fresh round of dollar selling, while boosting crypto and gold. In a blog post on Friday, hedge fund billionaire Ray Dalio warned of a looming debt crisis and said investors should be “underweighting debt assets like bonds, and overweighting gold and a bit of Bitcoin.” The so-called debasement trade is a strategy that involves moving capital away from fiat currency and sovereign debt toward scarcer assets such as gold and bitcoin. The move is considered a hedge against a potential weakening of the dollar.
Key Background
Last week, President Donald Trump hosted several crypto executives at the White House, giving another boost to the crypto surge. At the event, Trump called on Congress to pass the long-stalled CLARITY Act, which is backed by the crypto industry and will establish legal guidelines on digital assets. The president said: “We need Congress to take the next step by passing the CLARITY Act, a fair version of the CLARITY Act…It’s a very, very powerful structured legislation which will keep us ahead of China, keep us ahead of everyone else.”

### Key Points

- Ether rose to $2,503, while major tokens including Solana, Binance Coin, XRP, and Dogecoin saw gains between 18% and 52%.
- Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced increased bond buybacks to address rising yields and national debt concerns.
- President Donald Trump recently met with crypto executives to advocate for the passage of the CLARITY Act to establish digital asset regulations.

### Why it Matters
