articles.title: Stock market today: S&P 500, Nasdaq futures recover in countdown to Nvidia earnings, Fed Jackson Hole summit
articles.author: Grace O'Donnell
articles.content:
Stock market today: Dow, S&P 500, Nasdaq rise as US-Canada trade tensions heat up, investors await Nvidia earnings
US stocks gained on Tuesday as investors brushed aside worries about new trade measures against Canada, even as Canada announced new retaliatory tariffs on US goods. Markets also continued to weigh looming Nvidia (NVDA) earnings and predictions for Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech as Fed chair.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) and the S&P 500 (^GSPC) rose by 0.3%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) advanced by 0.6%, recovering from Monday's tech declines.
Nvidia stock rose 2% ahead of its highly anticipated quarterly results due out on Wednesday, snapping a seven-day losing streak.
Stocks held on to gains as a trade spat between the US and Canada escalated, with Canada's Finance Department announcing retaliatory tariffs to counter the 50% duties imposed by the Trump administration over the weekend. Notably, as the US and Canada have ratcheted up their rhetoric, they have left oil off the table for now, even as they raise tariffs on steel, dairy, and other products.
The price of bitcoin (BTC-USD), meanwhile, briefly surged above $80,000 for the first time in three months after the Treasury's intervention in the bond market revived concerns about dollar debasement, sending investors to alternative assets. Gold (GC=F), too, continued its march higher.
The latest economic data releases showed that both new home sales and a measure of consumer confidence fell to their lowest levels since January as cost-of-living pressures weighed on consumers. The data sets the stage for the Federal Reserve's Jackson Hole Symposium later this week, where Fed Chairman Warsh will deliver a speech.
Intuit (INTU) and Zoom Communications (ZM) will deliver key reads on the software sector when they report earnings on Tuesday, and DICK's Sporting Goods (DKS) stock sank 30% after the retailer missed second quarter expectations and cut its full-year outlook due to challenging conditions in the athletic marketplace.
- Grace O'DonnellStocks rise as bond yields fall. Nvidia snaps losing streak.US stocks rose, driven by falling Treasury yields and oil prices and gains across the tech sector. The 10-year Treasury yield (^TNX) dropped 6 basis points to 4.63%, while the 30-year yield (^TYX) fell to 5.17%. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) and the S&P 500 (^GSPC) added 0.3%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) rose 0.6%. Chip stocks gained momentum during Tuesday’s trading as investors rotated back into growth names and positioned ahead of Nvidia’s (NVDA) heavily scrutinized earnings report due out Wednesday. Nvidia (NVDA) stock itself gained 2%, snapping a seven-day losing streak. Here’s a look at how the major S&P 500 sectors performed, according to an AlphaSpace heatmap.
- Jake ConleyIMF chief says governments need to focus on tackling 'fiscal problems'Director of the International Monetary Fund Kristalina Georgieva said Tuesday that governments need to focus their efforts on addressing mounting fiscal concerns as national debts and deficits balloon. "All countries need to tackle their fiscal problems and formulate and present credible plans to ensure their debt and deficits are on sustainable path," Georgieva said in comments to reporters on Tuesday, reported by Bloomberg. The comments from the head of the international lender come at a precarious fiscal moment for the US, where national debt has reached $40 trillion and the country's debt-to-GDP ratio has climbed to 6%. Taking focus over the past few weeks has been a seemingly unstoppable run-up in Treasury yields, where the long end of the curve has held onto decades-long highs even as the Department of the Treasury intervenes. A surprise buyback announcement from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent last Thursday sent yields falling for the day, only for the rates to boomerang back up to where they were, which economists have interpreted as a sign the market is simply demanding higher returns to hold government obligations. Notably silent from the bond market arena has been Federal Reserve chairman Kevin Warsh, who has kept the FOMC focused squarely on inflation ahead of his first keynote address in Jackson Hole on Friday. Warsh's commitment to controlling inflation aligns with comments from Georgieva, who said "central banks must be laser focused on their price stability mandates" in her comments on Tuesday. Citing price stability threats facing the market, the IMF chief said, "We have literally a tug of war between the negative supply shock from the Middle East and the positive demand shock from AI."
- Grace O'DonnellSpaceX stock climbs after Elon Musk moves up orbital data center launch to 2027SpaceX (SPCX) stock gained altitude on Tuesday after Elon Musk pushed up the timeline for its AI satellites to launch into space. The company now expects them in orbit as soon as next year. Yahoo Finance’s Pras Subramanian reports: The SpaceX (SPCX) CEO took to X to update the timeline for launching the rocket company's first AI-powered satellites. "SpaceX, in partnership with Nvidia, has designed a space-optimized Vera Rubin NVL72 system for launch to orbit in Q4 next year, with significant scale in 2028," Musk said in a post on Monday afternoon. Musk's post comes on the heels of yesterday's announcement that SpaceX and Nvidia (NVDA) would be deploying Nvidia Vera processors "to accelerate the orchestration, code execution, and data processing that powers its next generation of agentic AI." The companies have worked together in the past and earlier this year announced that Nvidia chips would power SpaceX's coming AI satellites, aka orbital data centers.
- Jake ConleyOpenAI says its Jalapeño chip outperformed Nvidia tech in benchmark testsOpenAI (OPAI.PVT) chip leader Richard Ho said the AI lab's new Jalapeño chip outperformed those from Nvidia (NVDA) in recent testing, only a day before Nvidia is set to report second quarter results. The Jalapeño semiconductor outperformed Nvidia's GB300 chip in benchmarks of how much work it can handle per unit of power and the speed at which it returns responses, Ho said. "Jalapeño delivers both higher throughput and lower latency with one architecture, where existing hardware systems often have to make a tradeoff between the two," OpenAI said in a press release. "For customers, that can mean faster responses, more responsive agents, and more reliable access as demand grows." Nvidia shares traded up by roughly 1.7% as investors look toward the company's results coming after the bell on Wednesday. The news comes as OpenAI has increasingly turned toward building and running its AI models on its own hardware, underscoring the competition for advantages in the hardware sector of the AI boom. "OpenAI can design models, products, serving software, chips, memory, networking, and systems together, using what we learn from real workloads to improve every layer of the stack," the company said. While the Jalapeño model outperformed Nvidia's GB300 chip, OpenAI's new offering wasn't tested against Nvidia's newest-generation Vera Rubin chips, Bloomberg reported. The chip is also not designed for AI model training, where Nvidia's technology has traditionally excelled.
- Grace O'DonnellCanada announces retaliatory tariffs on roughly $20 billion in US goodsCanada said Tuesday it will match new 50% US tariffs “dollar for dollar” with counter tariffs beginning Sept. 8, affecting roughly $20 billion in imports. The Canadian tariffs will range from 15% to 50% on various targeted products, including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics. The Canadian rates will match the corresponding US tariff rates. “This focused response will protect Canadian workers, farmers, fishers, families, and businesses, defend industries harmed by unjustified U.S. tariffs, and help Canadian producers compete with U.S. products in the Canadian market,” the Canadian Finance Department said in a statement. Canada also announced an additional $7.5 billion in aid to workers and businesses impacted by the trade dispute. The move marks the latest escalation between the two neighboring countries. Earlier on Tuesday, President Trump lashed out at Canada on Truth Social, saying the country “has been ‘Ripping Off’ the U.S.A. for decades.” “I deal with many countries, and Canada is easily the most difficult and unreasonable,” Trump said.
- Jake ConleyConsumer confidence falls to lowest level since JanuaryConsumer confidence fell in August to the lowest level seen since January as cost-of-living pressures and a slowed hiring rate weighed on Americans' impression of the economy, just months away from critical midterm elections. The overall consumer confidence index fell to 89.4 from 90.8 in the previous month, while economists had been looking for 90.2. An index measuring expectations also fell, measuring at 68.2 against the previous month's reading of 74.7. Economists had expected a reading of 74.2. In the lone bright spot of the report from the Conference Board, readings on the present situation index rose month over month to 121.1 from 114.9. The measure also beat economists' expectations of 114.7. "Consumer confidence moderated slightly in August for a second consecutive month," said Dana Peterson, chief economist at the Conference Board. "Looking ahead, consumers were more pessimistic about business conditions and the labor market over the next six months. Expectations for household incomes moderated but remained optimistic overall."
- Jake ConleyNew home sales fall to lowest level since JanuaryUS new home sales fell to the lowest level since January as heightened mortgage rates have proven sticky, turning away prospective buyers. Signings on new single-family homes fell to an annualized rate of 607,000, down from the previous month's 628,000. Economists had been looking for a rate of 620,000 sales, per Bloomberg. As housing prices and mortgage rates have stayed high, new home sales have declined in three of the last four months, data from the US Census Bureau showed.
- Jake ConleyApple shares hold flat after Mac Mini and Mac Studio release newsApple (AAPL) shares began the day trading largely flat despite the news that fresh versions of the company's Mac Mini and Mac Studio are coming to market. Our Daniel Howley reports: On Tuesday, the company debuted new versions of each pint-sized desktop with more performance aimed at AI developers. The Mac Mini gained traction among AI enthusiasts and engineers thanks to its relatively low cost and ability to operate without a display. That made it ideal for running AI agents that handle tasks for developers, who can control them on the go from their smartphones or laptops. The Mac Studio also drew engineers who didn't necessarily need a display, as well as for its powerful chips. The latest Mac Mini launches with Apple's all-new M6 processor or the M5 Pro chip. The M6 version can be outfitted with up to 32GB of memory, while the M5 Pro gets up to 64GB. The Mac Studio gets Apple's M5 Max and new M5 Ultra processors. Apple promises big leaps in overall AI performance for both systems, as well as improved capabilities around gaming and video editing.
- Grace O'DonnellStocks gain as oil and bond yields fallStocks rose on Tuesday, downplaying US tensions with Canada and Iran. The Dow Jones Industrial Average (^DJI) and the S&P 500 (^GSPC) rose 0.4%. The tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) rose by a stronger 0.7%. Here's a check of the markets in the first few minutes of trading, based on a heat map powered by Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. Bitcoin (BTC-USD) traded at $79,000 per token. Oil prices dropped 3%, with WTI crude sitting above $82 per barrel and Brent (BZ=F) hovering near $88 per barrel. The 10-year Treasury yield (^TNX) fell 5 basis points to 4.64%. The 30-year yield (^TYX) declined to 5.18%.
- Grace O'DonnellNvidia stock is on a 7-day losing streak ahead of its big earnings reportInvestors are dumping Nvidia (NVDA) heading into its closely watched earnings report on Wednesday evening, Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi points out. He writes: Nvidia stock has fallen for seven straight trading days, per Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. The sell-off marks the stock's longest losing streak since 2022. The stock has lost about 7% over this stretch, compared with a 1.2% drop for the S&P 500 (^GSPC). The Nvidia bulls may be looking to avoid one harsh reality, at least from a short-term perspective. Strong earnings reports haven't been too kind to Nvidia's stock of late. Nvidia stock has fallen in response to earnings in six of the past eight quarters, including the last four, per Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace analysis.
- Grace O'DonnellDick's Sporting Goods stock tanks 14% after retailer cuts guidanceDick’s Sporting Goods (DKS) stock fell 14% in premarket trading after the retailer posted disappointing second quarter results and lowered its full-year outlook. The company said that competitors heavily discounting items, fewer product launches, and those launches underperforming expectations created “challenging conditions” for the retailer. As a result, Dick’s slashed its full-year outlook for diluted earnings per share to $10.94 to $11.94, down from its previous forecast of $13.27 to $14.27. The 2026 net sales guidance of $21.9 billion to $22.2 billion was also cut from the previous $22.1 billion to $22.4 billion. The company maintained its same-store sales guidance for its Dick’s business at 2.5% to 4.0% growth, but slightly lowered expectations for Foot Locker's same-store sales growth to negative 2.0% to 0.0%. In the most recent quarter, Dick’s reported comparable sales growth of 2.1%, down from 2.5% in the same quarter a year ago, with the Foot Locker business dragging down growth. Second quarter adjusted earnings per share came in at $3.53 on revenue of $5.58 billion. That missed Wall Street’s expectations of earnings of $3.76 on revenue of $5.64 billion, per S&P Global Market Intelligence.
- Jared BlikreSoftware is crushing chips by a record marginSoftware stocks are near record highs. Chips are still stuck in a bear market — except Nvidia (NVDA) never really joined them. The handoff happened almost to the day. Chip stocks peaked on June 22. Software bottomed right around then, kicking off a multitrillion-dollar reversal that has sent the two groups in almost perfectly opposite directions. Strip out the megacaps, and the symmetry is wild. The equal-weight SPDR S&P Software & Services ETF (XSW) is up about 24% since then, while the equal-weight SPDR S&P Semiconductor ETF (XSD) is down about 24%. That near-50-percentage-point gap is the widest comparable software-over-chips move in the ETFs' history back to 2011. And this is not an index quirk.
- Grace O'DonnellWhy the US and Canada have been reluctant to hit the oil switch in their trade spatYahoo Finance’s Jake Conley reports: A breakdown in trade negotiations between the US and Canada over the weekend led Washington to impose a 50% tariff on a wide range of Canadian goods, including furniture, dairy, electrical products, and plywood. But the tariffs specifically exclude one of the most critical products crossing the border between the two countries: crude oil. The US is by far the largest buyer of Canadian crude, accounting for 90% of Canada's crude exports in 2025, or roughly 126 billion Canadian dollars of a total CA$140 billion. The dependence runs in both directions: Canada supplied roughly 63% of all US crude imports last year. Those figures reflect a North American oil industry that has become deeply integrated over decades, particularly between Alberta's oil fields and US refineries.

Here's what's happening today.Economic data: ADP weekly employment change, week ended Aug. 8; Philadelphia Fed non-manufacturing activity, August (7.4 previously); FHFA house price index, month-on-month, June (+0.3% previously); Richmond Fed manufacturing index, August (5 previously); Richmond Fed business conditions, August (-5 previously); New home sales, month-on-month, July (+1.6% previously); Conference Board consumer confidence, August (90.8 previously); Conference Board present situation, August (114.9 previously); Conference Board expectations, August (74.7 previously) Earnings calendar: Bank of Montreal (BMO.TO), Intuit (INTU), Zoom Communications (ZM), DICK's Sporting Goods (DKS) Catch up on some stories you might have missed overnight:

Brent crude futures rose 27 cents, or 0.3%, to $92.44 a barrel by 0330 GMT, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate crude was up 37 cents, or 0.4%, at $85.38. Both contracts settled lower on Monday, with U.S. crude oil falling to a one-week low on profit taking after prices rallied over the previous two weeks. articles.title: Be Quiet! Light Mount TKL review
articles.author: Jess Kinghorn
articles.content:
Our Verdict
Still just as quiet, still looking great, but now in a more space-saving form factor with SOCD. Beyond that though, other small keyboards leave the Light Mount TKL's offering of gaming features in the dust.
For
- Somehow even quieter switches
- Great typing feel
- One classy looking keyboard
Against
- Not as fully featured as other TKL gaming keyboards
- PBT keycaps don't allow for the brightest RGB
PC Gamer's got your back
My prime PC gaming hours tend to be when the rest of my household is already in bed. As such, the fantastically clicky-clacky key presses of a mechanical gaming keyboard echoing through our halls isn't really ideal. It's just as well then that Be Quiet! is back with a welcome update to the very nearly silent keyboard I loved last year, the Light Mount.
As someone with a perennially messy desk, the Light Mount TKL's 80% size is just right; I have room to swish my mouse, and I find I'm not forever accidentally hitting the capslock key as with other cut-down keebs. This TKL update offers more than just a smaller form factor, though, introducing the next generation of Be Quiet!'s Silent switches in Linear and Tactile flavours.
This TKL update also addresses one of the key problems I had with the original Light Mount by introducing new gaming features. This includes Quick Tap (SOCD), which will be sweet percussion to the ears of shooter fans—and at best eyebrow raising for the esports sickos. For those unfamiliar, SOCD stands for 'Simultaneous Opposing Cardinal Directions'. Features falling under this umbrella, like Razer's Snap Tap and now Be Quiet!'s Quick Tap, prioritises your most recent directional input, making for strafing so efficient that Valve banned it from Counter-Strike 2.
Alongside Quick Tap, there's also more options for macros, and a few fresh customisation options within the IO center software. While I appreciate these additions and expansions, the TKL still isn't the most feature-packed gaming keyboard you'll find.
I still love the even-quieter switches, though. Coupled with the TKL's sturdy construction, this makes for another smart-looking package. However, it's rocking up to the rowdy PC gaming party as the quiet kid in the corner—that is to say, while some will definitely appreciate its charms, it can't compete with the louder, more popular keeb crowd.
Buy if...
✅ You want something that's actually quiet: If clackier keyboards are just too loud, this is the one for you. Better yet, the new V2 Silent switches are even quieter than their predecessors.
✅ You want a keyboard for both work and play: This board's smart looks mean it will be just as at home in the office as it is next to your RGB-illuminated rig.
Don't buy if...
❌  You're looking for a gaming keyboard that's the complete package: Though this does bring a few new things to Be Quiet's table, it's less fully-featured than other TKL options.
❌ You're working with an extremely limited amount of desk space: As an 80% keyboard, you can definitely go smaller.
Still just as quiet, still looking great, but now in a more space-saving form factor with SOCD. Beyond that though, other small keyboards leave the Light Mount TKL's offering of gaming features in the dust.
Features
|  | Be Quiet! Light Mount TKL | 
| Switch | Be quiet! Silent V2 Linear Mechanical Switches (Tactile also available) | 
| Size | 80% | 
| Connection type | Wired | 
| Cable | Braided USB Type-C/USB Type-A | 
| Onboard storage | Yes | 
| Backlight | RGB LED | 
| Media controls | Tactile knob, twist for volume control, tap top to mute | 
| Wristrest | Yes, magnetic attachment | 
| Keycaps | PBT, double-shot | 
| Weight | 770 g | 
| Price | $140/€140 | 
The Light Mount TKL is an 80% keyboard that enjoys the latest generation of Be Quiet!'s Silent switches. Tactile switches are available, but my review unit came with the Silent Linear V2s (though if you're craving clicky-ness, the media knob in the keyboard's top left corner has got you covered). According to Be Quiet!, the new V2s feature thicker gold contact points for the copper lever inside, as well as 'optimised lubrication for quieter operation and improved responsiveness'—well, I'll be the judge of that.
The V1 switches were already astonishingly understated on the full-sized board, making the most of the original Light Mount's internal layers of sound dampening. The V2 switches on the TKL are somehow even quieter.
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.
Though the new switches feel a bit on the firm side right out of the box, they soon actuate just as cleanly as the V1s. Before, I described typing on the Tactile V1s as a controlled descent onto solid ground, but the Linear V2s have a little more pleasing texture underhand. It's not like stepping on a discordantly crunchy leaf, it's more like tiptoeing over a thin layer of soft sand—I like it!
The combination of the V2s and the TKL's construction also means the space bar is now much quieter than what I found on this board's big brother. Although, it's worth noting that future productions of both the full size Light Mount and the Dark Mount will come with the new V2 switches.
So far, so excellent: the Light Mount TKL is an actually quiet mechanical keyboard that won't tattle on you during late night gaming sessions. So, what about those fresh gaming features? Well, let's get the least exciting addition out of the way first: You can now disable the Capslock key in Game Mode.
Cool. Moving swiftly on, the Light Mount TKL also enjoys Be Quiet's version of SOCD, Quick Tap, for the first time. Whereas the original Light Mount felt more like a fairly quiet mechanical keyboard you could also use for gaming, the TKL feels a smidge more like a gaming keyboard in its own right.
And you know what gamers love above all else? Bathing themselves in the glow of RGB lighting. Like its predecessors, the TKL implementation of RGB is similarly classy; a dedicated light strip lines the very top of the keyboard, and every switch below enjoys an 'ARGB diffuser' for tasteful per-key illumination. On top of plenty of customisation options in the IO Center software, the Light Mount TKL also features support for Microsoft Dynamic Lighting.
Performance
The Be Quiet! Light Mount TKL is a joy to type on. Switch-feel is really second to none in my mind. But what about gaming? Well, as I've said before, my most intense encounter in an online game recently was getting lost in Big Walk (not to mention how I tend to spend more time hiding in bushes in Arc Raiders than running and gunning). Similarly, this isn't a gaming keyboard with the competitive scene in mind. With those expectations set, let's get into it.
I tend to accidentally hit the Capslock key on smaller form factor keyboards, such as the Cherry XTRFY K5 Pro TMR Compact. The option to disable this key in Game Mode is definitely welcome, though I do find myself stumbling on to Capslock a lot less with this TKL. I also found this keyboard's layout and 1,000 Hz maximum polling rate does little to impede my running around the feline-themed post office of Cat Mail Co. The Shift key for sprinting between barely organised shelves is comfortably within reach—so long as you don't subconsciously curl your hand into a weird cat paw-esque grip like I do.
The TKL's precision is definitely welcome as I roll up everything in sight in Once Upon a Katamari. The TKL's responsiveness already makes it easy to both slow my roll and steer clear of disaster. Quick Tap comes especially in handy here, making changing the direction of my Katamari all the snappier. Does that mean I start immediately smashing through all of my previous records? Eh, no, not exactly. A swish gaming keyboard can only do so much for a skill issue, after all.
Whether I'm whiling away the wee hours trying to improve my Katamari game, or simply lose track of time playing Paralives, the Light Mount TKL's luscious layers of sound-dampening foam and updated Silent switches continue to keep the secret of my late night gaming sessions.
Build Quality
This is a lovingly put together keyboard. I've already waxed lyrical about the factory-lubricated V2 Silent switches and their lovely, linear actuation. The keys themselves aren't completely smooth on top, offering a little bit of surface texture that's typical of PBT caps. This choice of material is generally more durable than ABS, and also tends to be much more resistant to picking up finger grease. In other words, these PBT keycaps will be looking box fresh for much longer.
Speaking of looks, you're not going to find the Light Mount TKL in any fun colourways. Normally, I would rue the lack of a lavender colourway, but I respect Be Quiet's vision; this is a smart looking keyboard that wouldn't be out of place in either a gamer den or an office with a strict dress code. Besides, if you're still desperate for a splash of colour, the IO Center software offers lots of customisation options for the RGB lighting.
A potentially unfortunate wrinkle is that PBT keycaps aren't known for letting a lot of light through. That means that, even with the keycaps' shine-through legends, the RGB lighting here is generally a more subtle affair. An arched ARGB diffuser on each switch keeps what glow there is evenly distributed, but I can't help but feel the original Light Mount's RGB was a smidge brighter.
Mind you, the gamer den I was testing the fullsize board in is generally much darker than the bright overhead lights of PCG towers where I spent most of my quality time with the TKL. Anyway, the strip of RGB at the top of the TKL is all the lovelier for being allowed to shine unimpeded.
Like the company's other boards, the TKL also enjoys three internal layers of sound-dampening foam. This makes good on the entire promise of Be Quiet! while also making for a keeb with a pleasing amount of sturdy heft. The same brushed aluminium top plate featured on Be Quiet's other boards is also the finishing touch here, acting as the shiny cherry topping an already beautifully constructed cake.
Software
IO Center can either be downloaded as a local desktop app, or accessed via the web. For the most part, it's a smartly laid out bit of software that makes it easy to tweak an array of settings. The latest version offers a helpful hardware monitor too, showing you temps and even fan RPM right there in the dashboard, though obviously this is less relevant in a review about a keyboard.
What is relevant is the robust selection of customisation options for the RGB lights. The usual rippling designs return, allowing for gradient, single, or dual colour lighting effects. If you aren't digging IO Center's 'general' pre-sets, you can create your own layered lighting, customising the look of each key and segment of the top light bar. The Light Mount TKL also enjoys support for Microsoft Dynamic Lighting for those with a much grander, all encompassing vision for their desk.
Now, obviously RGB lighting isn't the only thing that makes a gaming keyboard. Via IO Center, you can also fine tune the Game Mode across a small selection of toggles. These allow you to disable various key configurations while the mode is active, including Shift + Tab, Alt + F4, the Windows Key, Alt + Tab, and now Capslock too.
Interestingly, Quick Tap falls outside of IO Center's Key Binding sub-menu. Instead, you'll find options for remapping keys, editing the Function layer, and recording a whole load of Macros.
Quick Tap is found under 'Product Settings,' alongside the Game Mode. Quick Tap can be calibrated across five key pairs ('A' and 'D' are included as an editable default pair to start you off). While in Quick Tap settings, the software also warns that some competitive titles will restrict or ban SOCD tech, and advises that you check the rules for your game of choice before calibrating.
Value
The Light Mount TKL costs $140/€140. That's about $30/€30 less than the full size version would set you back at launch, though you can get a 100% Light Mount for much less now. That's just as well, as the full size version graces our best gaming keyboards guide as our pick for the best silent board. The obvious question, then, is does the TKL do enough to dethrone its older sibling?
Well, the TKL introduces a number of features that will be coming to future productions of the full size keyboard, such as the V2 switches. Those who already have the full size Light Mount will also be able to enjoy the slightly expanded Game Mode through updates to IO Center, though Be Quiet is still evaluating if further features will be added retroactively.
What I can tell you for sure right now is, due to technical limitations, neither the full size Light Mount or Dark Mount will have the TKL's 10 customisable layers of lighting effects, or its ability to record up to 999 Macro events. The original Light Mount is limited to 58, while the Dark Mount can record up to 200. So, if you use a lot of complex Macros and are looking for a quiet keeb, the TKL is the gaming keyboard to go with.
But that's the thing: many PC gamers will tell you 'the clack is the whole point' of a mechanical keyboard. Personally, I think there's room for a range of sound profiles in this space, but the Light Mount TKL's central reason for being is arguably niche in appeal.
As an 80% design, the TKL is far from the most space-saving thing either, plus plenty of smaller boards beat it on features, too. For instance, our pick for the best 75% keyboard is the Keychron K2 HE, which comes with Hall effect switches and offers customisable actuation points. It's also wireless, woody, and basically the same price as Be Quiet's slightly larger offering.
If you're looking to save yet more desk space, our pick for the best 60% keyboard is the Wooting 60HE v2, which our Jacob describes as "the best keyboard that Wooting has ever made." That's high-praise that feels absolutely earned once you hear just how feature-packed it is.
You can also get a feature-packed 65% gaming keyboard for much less than the Light Mount TKL. Case in point, the best budget gaming keyboard is the Gamakay x NaughShark NS68, and having spent some quality time with this $40 keyboard myself, going with something 100 bucks more feels like a steep ask.
Obviously, a $40 keyboard cannot hold a candle to Be Quiet's build quality, and its software also leaves a lot to be desired compared to IO Center's ease of use. But otherwise the NS68 still offers fantastic value for money with Hall effect switches and even PBT keycaps.
As a typist, I still love the Light Mount TKL; the switches really are that quiet and the key actuation is wonderfully smooth. Though I rue the lack of fun colourways, the aluminium topped chassis definitely looks very classy as it is, and I appreciate all of the options for colourful RGB customisation in the IO Center software. Although not the brightest, the RGB here illuminates my dank gamer den well enough.
As a PC gamer, I am left wanting just a little more for the money—specifically, the option to customise key actuation points wouldn't go amiss. To be fair, having seen how much the full size Light Mount has come down in price since its launch last year, the TKL may also drop to a similarly appealing price point before too long.
Furthermore, I'm hardly a high-tier competitive gamer and what's here on the TKL definitely suits most of my gaming needs. If you can take or leave gaming keyboards' bleeding edge features, but still want a well-made mechanical keyboard to class up your desk, there's lots to like about the Light Mount TKL.

articles.title: Discord is yet to be served Take-Two's GTA 6 leak subpoena, which is set to demand broad access to user data
articles.author: Sherif Saed
articles.content:
Discord has said that it has not yet been served a subpoena from Take-Two regarding Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks. On Friday, it was reported that the Rockstar parent company filed multiple subpoenas in a federal district court in order to obtain a wide range of user data from Discord and Microsoft relating to the leaks.
Some Discord users fear the scope of the subpoena is so broad it potentially affects all users of the Discord servers where the leaks circulated, which number in the hundreds of thousands.
Discord's marketing director, Ryan K. Rigney, has now responded, saying that the company has not yet received a subpoena from Take-Two, and that every request will be evaluated
"I can share an update on this: Discord has not yet been served with a subpoena from Take-Two," K. Rigney wrote on X on Monday. "When we do, we'll evaluate the validity and scope before responding."
It's worth noting that filing a subpoena is separate to actually serving a party with one, and that companies are not required to respond to a subpoena until they have been formally served it. The subpoena itself has been filed by Take-Two, and so it would seem Discord is simply yet to receive an actual formal service.
According to the filing, Take-Two is requesting data that includes registration emails, registration and last-login IP addresses, phone numbers, linked connections and associated device identifiers for "all user accounts that are/were members" of multiple Discord community servers, including Ødyssey.gg, "! Odyssey", and DarkViperAU from 1st June.
On Friday, Bloomberg reporter Jason Schreier said that Rockstar had yet to learn the identity of the leaker or work out how the breach occurred. According to a person familiar with the company's plans, the leak won't affect this week's planned Netflix extended look.
Microsoft was the other company named in the subpoena. Specifically, Take-Two wanted OneDrive data - the online storage platform where some of the leaks were hosted - as well as the Xbox accounts linked to users' Discord accounts.
Meanwhile, Xbox CTO Scott Van Vliet said that Microsoft is co-operating with Take-Two and Rockstar. "We are working closely with Take-Two and Rockstar Games to support efforts to protect creative works and intellectual property," Van Vliet said on X.
Take-Two's request gave Discord and Microsoft until 4th September to produce the necessary information. Over the last several days, GTA 6 suffered a number of leaks. Small gameplay videos emerged showing a new carjacking mechanic, a six-star Wanted system, driving around the city at night, NPC behaviour and cop chases. The game's full map appears to have also been leaked, alongside other smaller bits of gameplay at various points of interest around the map.
articles.summary:
Discord has confirmed it has not yet been served a subpoena by Take-Two Interactive regarding the recent unauthorized leaks of Grand Theft Auto 6 gameplay footage and data.

### Key Points
- Take-Two Interactive filed subpoenas seeking user data from Discord and Microsoft to identify the source of recent Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks.
- Requested information includes registration emails, IP addresses, phone numbers, and device identifiers for members of specific Discord servers like Ødyssey.gg.
- Discord marketing director Ryan K. Rigney stated the company will evaluate the validity and scope of any request once formally served.
- Microsoft confirmed it is cooperating with Take-Two and Rockstar Games to protect intellectual property, specifically regarding OneDrive and Xbox account data.
- The subpoena filing sets a deadline of September 4 for the requested information to be produced by the tech companies.

### Why it Matters
This legal action highlights the aggressive measures major publishers take to identify leakers and protect unreleased intellectual property from widespread distribution. The broad scope of the request raises significant privacy concerns for hundreds of thousands of users who may be caught in the investigation despite having no involvement in the breach.

articles.title: Fake Minecraft Clients Deliver WeedHack Malware Despite Infrastructure Takedown
articles.author: Kevin  Poireault
articles.content:
A large-scale malware-spreading scheme targeting Minecraft players has continued to evolve despite the takedown of the threat actor’s malicious infrastructure in July.
In a new report, researchers at McAfee shared that over 6300 attempts to access malicious sites linked to the ‘WeedHack’ malware campaign were blocked by McAfee WebAdvisor in the past month.
WeedHack is a malware-as-a-service (MaaS) campaign spotted by McAfeee in July.
It utilized SEO poisoning techniques and malicious websites impersonating legitimate Minecraft clients and infected over 116,464 gamers with malware.
While the initial infrastructure underlying the campaign, including the command-and-control (C2) server, was taken down by McAfee in July, the researchers noticed that the campaign was still active in August.
“Consequently, we have observed a shift in tactics by these attackers,” McAfee researchers said, noting that threat actors have increasingly pivoted to file-hosting services such as Discord to distribute WeedHack.
Discord accounted for 49.6% of the links associated with WeedHack deployments identified by the cybersecurity firm, followed by MediaFire (23.4%), GitHub (8.2%), and Dropbox (4.6%).
The remaining URLs were customer-facing websites impersonating Minecraft resellers, sometimes offering paid tools for free to lure users into clicking on malicious links.
“In one case, the top two Google results observed by researchers for a popular Minecraft client led to sites distributing WeedHack, demonstrating how SEO poisoning can put malicious downloads directly in gamers’ paths,” the researchers wrote.
Researchers also identified a malicious site built using an AI-powered website creation platform.
To avoid falling into the trap the threat actor has set up for them, McAfee researchers recommended that gamers download mods, clients and other files only from trusted, official sources, while avoiding suspicious offers such as free versions of paid tools or cracked software.
They also advised keeping security software enabled, scanning downloads before opening them and checking URLs carefully for lookalike domains that could lead to malicious sites.

articles.summary:
The WeedHack malware campaign continues to target Minecraft players by shifting distribution tactics to file-hosting services after security researchers dismantled the operation's original command-and-control infrastructure in July.

### Key Points
- McAfee researchers blocked over 6,300 attempts to access malicious WeedHack sites in the past month.
- The campaign has infected more than 116,464 gamers by impersonating legitimate Minecraft clients through SEO poisoning.
- Attackers now primarily distribute malware via Discord, which accounts for 49.6% of identified malicious links.
- Other distribution channels include MediaFire, GitHub, Dropbox, and websites mimicking official Minecraft resellers.
- Threat actors are utilizing AI-powered platforms to rapidly create deceptive websites that lure users with free versions of paid software.

### Why it Matters
This campaign highlights the persistent threat of malware-as-a-service models that quickly adapt to infrastructure takedowns by leveraging popular, trusted file-hosting platforms. Gamers remain at significant risk from SEO poisoning, necessitating increased vigilance when downloading third-party mods or software from unofficial sources.

articles.title: Python Software Foundation: Georgi Ker: 2026 PSF Board Election Candidate Interview
articles.author: Marie Nordin
articles.content:
Who are you?
Hi, I’m Georgi, an independent entrepreneur, open source community organiser, and leader. I’m also a PSF Fellow and a recipient of the PSF Community Service Award.
Although I currently live in Amsterdam, I am proud to represent communities across Asia. I have served on the PSF Board since 2023. I also helped design PyCon US branding and websites since 2022 and for other open source community events and projects as well.
My contributions to the Python community span over many years, beginning mainly in Asia and becoming more international over time. Much of my work sits where people, governance, and community meet.
I care especially about the people doing the quiet work that keeps open source communities alive. They may not always be on the main stage, but the community would not exist without them.
What would you bring to the PSF Board of Directors?
Three years on the Board have taught me where the PSF is strong, where it is fragile, and where good intentions are not becoming results. 
As a former Treasurer, I raised concerns about the lack of a clear financial runway and pushed for stronger budgeting and regular financial planning. Through the Executive Committee, I have also participated in staff discussions, document reviews, difficult organisational decisions, and helped finalize the PSF’s long-delayed strategic planning process with the board.
My perspective is also strongly shaped by communities around the world. The work began from Asia and now includes PyLadiesCon, EuroPython, and regular discussions with global community leaders through the PSF Diversity and Inclusion Workgroup. Global representation at the PSF has improved, but it still remains incomplete.
I would bring institutional knowledge, experience in financial oversight and a global community perspective. And yes, I am willing to do the unglamorous work. 
I know more now than when I joined. I know what I am signing up for and how much work remains.
What motivated you to run for the PSF Board of Directors?
I am running because the past three years have shown me much more clearly what the PSF needs next. I’ve seen where the Foundation works well. I’ve also seen outdated financial assumptions, limited organisational capacity, unclear responsibilities, and decisions that could not be implemented because the necessary systems or that expertise were missing.
These are not exciting campaign topics but unfortunately, they matter.
Python is now part of the world’s infrastructure. Companies, governments, researchers, schools, and millions of developers depend on it. The organisation responsible for protecting Python must be able to plan beyond the next conference or sponsorship cycle.
I would like to continue helping the PSF build a more realistic base, improve its financial planning, strengthen its internal systems, and communicate more honestly with the community.
The next few years matter. That is why I am running again.
What problem or challenge do you want to address if you are on the Board?
The problem I most want to address is the PSF’s financial sustainability.
For years, PyCon US was a reliable source of income for the Foundation. After COVID, the economics and risks of large conferences changed. PyCon US should remain an important community event, but one conference should not be expected to carry the financial future of the organisation protecting Python.
The PSF needs realistic budgets and financial projections. The Board needs to understand the Foundation’s runway, commitments, risks, and future operating costs. Hope is useful in open source but less useful in accounting.
We also need to build sponsorship around Python itself. Companies benefit from Python every day, not only when their logo appears at a conference. Their support should help fund Python’s infrastructure, security, legal protection, trademarks, and global community.
This requires a serious review of the PSF’s business model. It also requires the right staff capacity and expertise to turn Board decisions into results.
I would like the PSF to professionalise the support around the community without professionalising the community out of Python. That distinction really matters. Volunteers and local organisers are not a cheap workforce. They are the reason Python has a community in the first place. 
Where do you see the PSF 5 years from now?
In five years, I would like to see the PSF be an organisation that plans with evidence instead of habit.
The PSF should be better equipped to protect Python’s trademarks, copyright, infrastructure, and identity. As Python becomes more important, this will require greater legal, financial, security, and organisational expertise. Goodwill alone cannot do all that work.
It should have a clear financial runway, realistic budgets, and dependable sources of income. PyCon US should continue bringing people together, but its financial performance should not decide whether the Foundation can support Python properly.
I would also like a more transparent PSF. The community should understand what the Board is working on, what the Foundation can afford, why major decisions were made, and what progress followed. 
Finally, the PSF should remain global and human. It should develop new leaders, support communities outside North America and Europe, and recognise capable people who may not be famous conference speakers. In fact, the board should consider reserving a few board seats for appointed directors with expertise that the Foundation needs.
The PSF should become more professional in how it operates without becoming corporate in how it treats people. Python’s community is not a side project. It is one of its greatest strengths and part of its unique model. 
What areas of the Python community are you involved with?
I have served on the PSF Board since 2023, including as Treasurer and currently as Vice Chair.
I currently chair the PSF Diversity and Inclusion Workgroup. I am also one of the organisers of PyLadiesCon and a member of the EuroPython Code of Conduct team. My earlier involvement included PyCon Thailand, PyCon APAC, founding PyLadies Bangkok, and other regional communities. I am also involved with the podcast PyPodcats featuring underrepresented Pythonistas.
Apart from that, I am developing Open Community Leadership through the fellowship with the Sovereign Tech Agency. The project focuses on mentorship, succession planning, sustainability, and helping communities prepare their next generation of leaders.
------

articles.summary:
PSF Board member Georgi Georgiev is seeking re-election to address the organization's financial sustainability and improve long-term operational planning for the Python programming language's global infrastructure.

### Key Points
- Georgi Georgiev has served on the Python Software Foundation (PSF) Board since 2023, previously acting as Treasurer and currently as Vice Chair.
- The candidate advocates for moving beyond reliance on PyCon US revenue by diversifying sponsorship models to fund core infrastructure and legal protections.
- Key policy goals include implementing evidence-based financial planning, increasing organizational transparency, and strengthening internal systems to support global community growth.
- Georgiev’s background includes leadership roles in PyLadiesCon, EuroPython, and various regional Python communities across Asia.
- The platform emphasizes professionalizing PSF operations while maintaining the community-driven, volunteer-focused nature of the Python ecosystem.

### Why it Matters
As Python becomes critical global infrastructure, the PSF faces increasing pressure to manage its resources and legal responsibilities more effectively. A shift toward sustainable financial models ensures the foundation can support the language's security and development without relying solely on conference cycles.

articles.title: Bitcoin Jumps Above $80,000 as ‘Debasement Trade’ Pressures Dollar
articles.author: Fiona Craig
articles.content:
© Adobe Stock Images
Bitcoin (COIN:BTCUSD) surged to its highest level in more than three months on Tuesday, as concerns over the health of U.S. public finances weighed on the dollar and encouraged investors to increase exposure to cryptocurrencies.
The world’s largest cryptocurrency climbed 4.7% to $80,760.8 by 01:57 ET (05:57 GMT), having briefly touched $81,220.4, its strongest level in three months.
The latest advance puts Bitcoin on course to record gains in eight of the past nine sessions following a sharp rebound over the previous week. Short-covering has provided additional momentum, with the rally forcing traders holding bearish positions to exit the market.
Much of Bitcoin’s latest strength has been linked to increasing concerns about U.S. fiscal policy and the longer-term outlook for the dollar.
Those worries intensified last week after the U.S. Treasury announced plans to roughly double the pace of its bond buybacks in an effort to contain the recent rise in yields.
The announcement prompted speculation that the dollar could come under pressure as the Treasury intervenes more actively in bond markets, encouraging what investors have described as the “debasement trade.”
“The Treasury’s buyback announcement has shifted the market narrative from higher yields to USD debasement – fuelling a weaker USD, stronger gold and higher breakevens. While QE comparisons are overdone, rising policy uncertainty and questions around Fed independence are weighing on the USD,” OCBC analysts said in a note.
The shift has increased investor interest in assets such as gold and cryptocurrencies, which are viewed by some market participants as offering protection from instability in government bond and currency markets.
Bitcoin has been a significant beneficiary of that trend. Its relatively weak year-to-date performance before the recent recovery has also attracted investors looking to buy at lower valuations.
The rapid recovery has caused substantial losses for traders betting against Bitcoin.
Coinglass data showed that more than $457 million of Bitcoin short positions were liquidated over the previous 24 hours as prices continued to climb.
The latest wave of liquidations follows similar activity last week, when Bitcoin’s sudden rebound wiped out billions of dollars in bearish positions.
The impact extended into other cryptocurrency markets. According to Coinglass, approximately $112.3 million of short positions in Ether were also liquidated during the past 24 hours.
The wider cryptocurrency market followed Bitcoin higher on Tuesday, with most major digital assets recording gains.
Ether, the world’s second-largest cryptocurrency, rose 2.2% to $2,510.0, while XRP also advanced 2.2%.
Solana was among the strongest performers, jumping 7.6%. Cardano gained 3.3%, while BNB increased 2.3%.
Performance among memecoins was mixed. Dogecoin rose 1.3%, while $TRUMP declined 1.5%.
The broad-based gains underline the improvement in cryptocurrency market sentiment, with dollar weakness, fiscal concerns and short-covering combining to drive renewed demand for digital assets.

articles.title: Samsung wants iPhone users to feel at home on Galaxy
articles.author: Danny Dorresteijn
articles.content:
Last updated: August 25th, 2026 at 14:29 UTC+02:00
The similarities may be more strategic than they seem.
Abhijeet Mishra / SamMobile
From One UI to iOS, or the other way around, Samsung and Apple are getting closer than ever. And while Apple is making some moves that are more friendly towards Android users, Samsung appears to be taking much bigger steps to make its devices feel familiar to people coming from an iPhone.
You can't really blame Samsung for it. People generally don't like change, especially when it comes to devices and software they use every single day. The more familiar something feels, the easier it is to switch to it.
So does Samsung copy Apple? To a certain extent, yes. Apple does the exact same thing in some areas, but we can't deny that Samsung is taking bigger and faster steps to close the gap between the Galaxy and iPhone experience.
According to leaked sketches of the camera island on Samsung's upcoming Galaxy S27 series, for example, the design has similarities to Apple's recent iPhones. This isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it does raise an interesting question: Is Samsung running out of ideas, or is it deliberately making Galaxy phones look and feel more familiar to iPhone users?
Apple's iOS still looks different from One UI. But Apple continues to add software features that Samsung and Android have offered for years. Samsung, on the other hand, has increasingly adopted design elements and interface choices that make One UI feel more familiar to someone coming from an iPhone.
That could make switching from an iPhone to a Galaxy considerably less intimidating. Most people already use many of the same apps regardless of which platform they are on. Instagram, WhatsApp, YouTube, Spotify, Netflix and countless other apps work largely the same way on both.
If the apps are familiar and the hardware and software are increasingly familiar as well, there is simply less for an iPhone user to relearn when moving to a Galaxy device.
Samsung is also making the actual process of moving from an iPhone easier. Starting with One UI 9, the upgraded Smart Switch can transfer data from an iPhone wirelessly without requiring the Smart Switch app to be installed on the iPhone.
It can also bring over more of the things that make a phone feel like your own, including passwords and passkeys, call history, Wi-Fi networks, accessibility settings and eSIM information.
Some of these improvements were made possible by a new iPhone-to-Android migration system Google developed with Apple and introduced with Android 17.
But Samsung is one of the first companies taking advantage of it, and the result fits perfectly with its apparent strategy: the less an iPhone user has to leave behind or set up again, the smaller the barrier to moving to Galaxy.
The walls between the two platforms are coming down in other ways as well. Google made Quick Share compatible with Apple's AirDrop, and that functionality has since expanded to Galaxy devices.
Apple, for its part, is allowing that interoperability with AirDrop, something that would have been difficult to imagine a few years ago considering how fiercely the two ecosystems compete.
This isn't something Samsung itself introduced, but it still works in Samsung's favour. The fewer barriers there are between Galaxy phones and iPhones, the easier it becomes for an iPhone user to consider switching without worrying about losing basic conveniences they have grown used to.
At the same time, Samsung is embracing magnetic accessories with official cases for its flagship phones, bringing the experience closer to what iPhone users already know from MagSafe. Apple, meanwhile, is expected to launch its first foldable phone this year and enter a category Samsung has dominated for years.
The more time passes, the clearer Samsung's direction seems to become. People don't want to relearn everything when they switch phones, and Samsung appears to understand that very well.
That may explain why Galaxy phones are increasingly borrowing ideas from Apple in both hardware and software. The goal may not simply be to copy Apple for the sake of copying it. Samsung may be trying to make an iPhone user pick up a Galaxy phone and immediately feel that the experience isn't as different as they expected.
Apple is making some moves in the opposite direction as well, particularly by allowing its ecosystem to become slightly friendlier towards Android. But Samsung clearly has more reason to reduce the differences. Every familiar design choice, software element, accessory and cross-platform feature removes another reason for an iPhone user to be afraid of switching.
And once the phone itself feels familiar, the biggest difference becomes the wider ecosystem around it: watches, earbuds, tablets, laptops and other devices.
It may not matter as much as it once did whether someone prefers iOS or One UI. What matters to Samsung is making sure an iPhone user can move to Galaxy without feeling like they have to start from scratch.
If that is indeed the strategy, Samsung's direction is becoming increasingly clear. And whether we like all of the similarities with Apple or not, it makes a lot of sense.
articles.summary:
Samsung is strategically aligning its Galaxy hardware and One UI software with Apple’s design language to lower the barrier for iPhone users switching to Android devices.

### Key Points
- Samsung’s upcoming Galaxy S27 series reportedly features camera island designs that mirror recent iPhone aesthetics.
- One UI 9 introduces an upgraded Smart Switch tool that transfers passwords, eSIM data, and call history from iPhones without requiring additional app installations.
- Samsung is adopting magnetic accessory standards for its flagship cases to replicate the convenience of Apple’s MagSafe ecosystem.
- Cross-platform interoperability has increased, with Google and Samsung integrating Quick Share to function alongside Apple’s AirDrop.
- The strategy leverages a new iPhone-to-Android migration system developed by Google and Apple to simplify the transition process for consumers.

### Why it Matters
By minimizing the learning curve for new users, Samsung is actively removing the friction that historically kept consumers locked into the Apple ecosystem. This shift suggests that hardware and software familiarity are becoming more critical to market competition than maintaining distinct, proprietary design identities.

articles.title: This Tiny USB Device Turns Your Phone Into a Keyboard, Mouse, and SSH Terminal
articles.author: Abhishek Prakash
articles.content:
Got a headless Raspberry Pi and want to connect to it? You don't need to use your computer for that. You can do that with your smartphone itself.
TechxArtisan's latest gadget turns your smartphone into a keyboard, mouse, gamepad and even a SSH terminal.
These folks gave us KVM-over-USB gadgets like Openterface Mini-KVM and Openterface KVM-GO in the past.
Now they are working on Openterface KeyMod, a tiny USB-bridge that can do a number of things by interacting with a computer from your phone.
Key Specifications
- Microcontroller: WCH CH32V208 RISC-V MCU
- USB functions: HID keyboard and mouse, plus a USB network bridge (SSH, VNC, file transfer), both active at the same time
- Wireless: BLE 5.3 on both models; KeyMod Plus adds a wired USB option for more bandwidth
- Phone app: KeyCmd, for Android (APK available) and iOS (coming soon)
- Two variants: Mini uses USB-C, Plus uses USB-A
Both variants have the same price tag of $24. The project is being crowdfunded on CrowdSupply.
The interesting thing here is not that the keyboard and mouse part. It's that KeyMod does two USB jobs at the same time. Let me explain.
You plug it into the target machine, and it shows up as a USB composite device: a standard HID keyboard and mouse, and a USB network bridge using the CDC-ECM standard, basically working as a private USB Ethernet link. The target gets a fixed IP at 192.168.11.2, your phone lands on 192.168.11.1. No DHCP, no Wi-Fi hunting, no driver to install on most systems.
Because HID input works without an OS loaded, KeyMod reaches BIOS screens, boot menus, and recovery environments too. It is similar to what Openterface Mini-KVM covers, just without the video feed.
On the phone side, the KeyCmd app decides what KeyMod does next. Their description mentions that KM Basic gives you a wireless keyboard, touchpad, and numpad. KM Pro adds a Shortcut Hub and Compose & Send, which lets you draft a long command, API key, or license key on your phone, review it, then fire it off as real keystrokes.
There's also Macros for scripted key sequences, a Presentation mode for Keynote and Google Slides, a Gamepad mode for emulators, and Shortcut Hub profiles for Blender, VS Code, etc.
Do note that KeyCmd is available only in APK format. It is not in Google Play Store. The iOS version has a 'coming soon' tag. I hope this thing is handled before the device gets shipped because Google plans to restrict sideloading of apps and Apple is notorious for raising fence to protect their walled garden.
Now, the network bridge is what makes Terminal (SSH) over BLE or USB possible, without needing a network setup. It works with macOS and Linux targets today. Windows support needs RNDIS instead of CDC-ECM, and that's still in development. Ah! That's so satisfactory as a Linux user ;)
Mini vs Plus
Mini and Plus run the same software, just connected differently.
KeyMod Mini is USB-C, BLE-only, and tiny enough for a keychain or phone lanyard at 25 x 15 x 5 mm and about 2.4 g.
KeyMod Plus is USB-A, adds a wired USB link to the phone for up to 10 Mbps (versus BLE's 2 Mbps), and is built more for staying plugged into servers, legacy PCs, or rack gear.
At $42, it lands close to InputStick ($34) and DexoPad ($39), but neither of those does SSH over BLE the way KeyMod does.
AI Agent Mode
Not only software, it seems like every hardware got to have AI these days.
So, there's also an experimental AI Agent Mode. You add your own LLM API key (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini, Ollama whatever you use), describe a goal in plain language like "check logs" or "restart service," and the model plans a sequence of terminal commands, presenting each one for your approval before it runs.
On newer iPhones (14 Pro and up), KeyCmd can also run a small local model instead, TechxArtisan says it has tested a 0.6B Qwen model under 1GB of RAM. It's clearly early, and TechxArtisan itself frames it as likely to stay experimental for a while.
Watch out for...
A couple of things you should know.
BLE encryption isn't turned on yet. The security design is finalized (Bluetooth LE Secure Connections, AES-128, ECDH P-256), but current beta and engineering kits ship without it enabled, with the actual switch-on coming through a firmware update before shipping.
If wireless exposure is a concern for your use case, KeyMod Plus's wired USB link bypasses BLE entirely during operation. CE and UKCA certification are also still in progress, though the company says both are committed before shipping.
On the open source side, KeyCmd for Android and iOS is in development for now and is slated to go fully open source on GitHub once the campaign wraps.
Hardware schematics and PCB files will be published as the project evolves, and OSHWA certification is planned, following Mini-KVM (CN000015) and KVM-GO (CN000022).
One more thing to set expectations on: this campaign's units will most likely ship in the current 3D-printed enclosure rather than an injection-molded one, since tooling would add at least two months to the timeline. Which, I think, means that the product may not look as smooth. If you have ever used 3D printed product, you will understand that.
Getting Openterface KeyMod
Openterface KeyMod is live on Crowd Supply. As of this writing it has raised $9,618 of its $15,000 goal (64%) from 149 backers, with funding closing on Oct 1, 2026.
Both the Mini and Plus are priced at $42, plus $8 shipping in the US or $18 worldwide. Orders placed now are estimated to ship Feb 14, 2027.

TechxArtisan has launched the Openterface KeyMod on CrowdSupply, a versatile USB-bridge device that allows users to control computers and manage headless servers directly from their smartphones.

### Key Points
- The device functions as a composite USB keyboard, mouse, and network bridge, enabling SSH access and file transfers without requiring existing Wi-Fi or DHCP configurations.
- It features a WCH CH32V208 RISC-V microcontroller and supports BLE 5.3, with the "Plus" model offering an additional wired USB connection for higher bandwidth.

This tool simplifies remote server management and hardware troubleshooting by eliminating the need for dedicated peripherals or complex network setups. By providing low-level access to BIOS and recovery environments via a smartphone, it offers a portable, efficient solution for IT professionals and Linux enthusiasts.

articles.title: Amazon Devices Just Got A Lot More Expensive Thanks To The Memory Crisis
articles.author: staff@bgr.com (Joshua Hawkins)
articles.content:
Amazon Devices Just Got A Lot More Expensive Thanks To The Memory Crisis
If you look at Amazon this week, you might notice that much of Amazon's hardware has become noticeably more expensive. The company quietly raised its prices across the board, including on devices like its Echo, Kindle, Fire TV, and eero lineups. While not every price hike is huge, there are some pretty substantial increases.
The Echo Dot has now jumped from $49.99 to $79.99 while Amazon's 16GB Kindle rose from $109.99 to $149.99. The 16GB Kindle Paperwhite increased from $159.99 to $199.99, too, and even the Fire TV Stick 4K Max has seen a hike, rising to $84.99 instead of its previous $59.99. Ring products weren't included in the increases at this time, however, but a number of the company's eero devices saw price hikes as well.
Amazon says rising component costs are the big bad to blame, with the company telling Fortune that the consumer electronics industry is dealing with "significant increases in memory and storage component costs." Much like the other companies that have followed this pattern in the past several months, Amazon claims that it had absorbed those costs for as long as it could before raising its prices.
Amazon isn't alone
Amazon might be the latest to raise hardware prices, but it has plenty of company. Roku raised prices on its streaming devices in July, with the company also blaming the rising memory prices as the primary driver. With Roku, these changes pose questions about the company's future as an affordable streaming platform, but Amazon doesn't face the same scrutiny. That's because its biggest devices — like Kindles — face some competition, but are largely in a powerful position in their respective market.
Other big tech companies such as Apple also raised prices, with the Mac, iPad, Apple TV, HomePod, and several other products getting a hike back in June. The base iPad went from $349 to $449, while the MacBook Neo increased from $599 to $699. The iPhone didn't see a price increase this time around, but it's likely only a matter of time until it does.
Samsung raised prices on a number of Galaxy phones, tablets, and laptops too. On phones, the increases mostly hit higher-storage configurations, with several 512GB and 1TB models going up by $80. Tablets were hit much harder, though, with the 512GB Galaxy Tab S11 climbing from $979.99 to $1,199.99. Meanwhile, the 1TB Galaxy Tab S11 Ultra jumped from $1,619.99 to $1,899.99. Samsung's laptops weren't spared either, with the 1TB Galaxy Book 6 Ultra increasing by $450, from $2,449.99 to $2,899.99.
Memory isn't getting cheaper, yet
Unfortunately, the price hikes are unlikely to stop there, either. TrendForce currently expects DRAM prices to jump another 13% to 18% quarter-over-quarter in Q3 2026, while NAND Flash prices are expected to climb between 10% to 15% higher than their current listings. As those prices increase on the manufacturer side, TrendForce expects that will trickle down to consumers even more, especially when looking at more expensive devices like laptops. In fact, we've already seen some companies discussing returning to 8GB of RAM as the standard for newer laptops in 2026 and onward.
The core of the problem, of course, is still AI. As data centers continue to expand and memory manufacturers shift more of their capacity toward creating server-based DRAM and high-bandwidth memory, the room for consumer-grace PC components is shrinking. And those areas of AI-focused manufacturing are expected to grow nearly 31% year over year in the most recent forecasts.
Adding more supply isn't something manufacturers can do overnight, either. Samsung, SK Hynix and other suppliers are already expanding production, but this takes time to build and ramp up. New DRAM capacity isn't expected to really make a meaningful difference until the second half of 2027, or the following year, while it's possible NAND could get relief sooner.
articles.summary:
Amazon has quietly increased prices across its Echo, Kindle, Fire TV, and eero hardware lineups, citing significant rising costs for memory and storage components within the electronics industry.

### Key Points
- The Echo Dot price increased from $49.99 to $79.99, while the 16GB Kindle rose from $109.99 to $149.99.
- Amazon attributed the hikes to industry-wide surges in memory and storage component costs that the company can no longer absorb.
- Other major tech firms, including Roku, Apple, and Samsung, have recently implemented similar price increases across their respective hardware portfolios.
- Market analysts at TrendForce project DRAM prices will rise another 13% to 18% in Q3 2026, further pressuring consumer electronics pricing.
- High demand for AI-focused server memory is limiting supply for consumer devices, with significant production relief not expected until late 2027 or 2028.

### Why it Matters
These widespread price hikes signal a sustained period of inflation for consumer electronics as manufacturers prioritize high-bandwidth memory for AI data centers. Consumers should expect continued cost increases and potential hardware downgrades, such as reduced RAM standards, until global production capacity catches up to demand.
